source_text: Comprobat hominis consilium fortuna, et cum unum omnes peterent, in ipso fluminis vado deprehensus Indutiomarus interficitur, caputque eius refertur in castra.
question: Quis Trevirorum princeps in ipso fluminis vado ab equitibus Labieni deprehensus et interfectus est?
question_en: Which chief of the Treveri was caught in the very ford of the river by Labienus's cavalry and killed?
derivation: Name fact anchored to the Treveri and Labienus; single named answer supported verbatim by 'in ipso fluminis vado deprehensus Indutiomarus interficitur'. The killing of Indutiomarus, instigator of the revolt, is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Sed de his duobus generibus alterum est druidum, alterum equitum.
question: Quae duo genera hominum honoratorum apud Gallos esse Caesar tradit?
question_en: Which two classes of honored men does Caesar report exist among the Gauls?
derivation: The famous fact that among Gauls of rank there are two privileged orders. Anchored to Caesar + the Gauls; single, verifiable two-name answer supported verbatim (alterum druidum, alterum equitum). Indirect statement (genera... esse) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Disciplina in Britannia reperta atque inde in Galliam translata esse existimatur, et nunc, qui diligentius eam rem cognoscere volunt, plerumque illo discendi causa proficiscuntur.
question: Ubi disciplinam druidum repertam esse Caesar tradit?
question_en: Where does Caesar report that the discipline of the druids was discovered?
derivation: Caesar's claim about the origin of druidic disciplina. Anchored to the druids; single place-name answer supported verbatim (in Britannia reperta). Indirect statement (disciplinam... repertam esse) under tradit; closed-book, oft-cited.

author: Caesar
source_text: Tantis excitati praemiis et sua sponte multi in disciplinam conveniunt et a parentibus propinquisque mittuntur. Magnum ibi numerum versuum ediscere dicuntur. Itaque annos nonnulli vicenos in disciplina permanent.
question: Quot annos nonnulli in druidum disciplina permaneant Caesar tradit?
question_en: How many years does Caesar report that some remain in the druids' training?
derivation: Length-of-training number fact. Anchored to the druidic disciplina; single number answer supported verbatim (annos... vicenos). Indirect question (permaneant, subj.) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Neque fas esse existimant ea litteris mandare, cum in reliquis fere rebus, publicis privatisque rationibus Graecis litteris utantur.
question: Quibus litteris Galli in publicis privatisque rationibus utantur Caesar scribit?
question_en: Which script does Caesar say the Gauls used for their public and private accounts?
derivation: Notable fact that, while not committing druidic lore to writing, the Gauls used Greek script for records. Anchored to the Gauls + accounts; verifiable answer supported verbatim (Graecis litteris utantur). Indirect question (utantur, subj.) under scribit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Deum maxime Mercurium colunt. Huius sunt plurima simulacra: hunc omnium inventorem artium ferunt, hunc viarum atque itinerum ducem, hunc ad quaestus pecuniae mercaturasque habere vim maximam arbitrantur.
question: Quem deum Gallos maxime colere Caesar tradit?
question_en: Which god does Caesar report the Gauls worship most?
derivation: The most-cited fact of the Gallic pantheon section. Anchored to Caesar + the Gauls; single name answer supported verbatim (Deum maxime Mercurium colunt). Indirect statement (Gallos colere) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Galli se omnes ab Dite patre prognatos praedicant idque ab druidibus proditum dicunt.
question: A quo deo Galli se omnes prognatos esse praedicant, ut Caesar scribit?
question_en: From which god do the Gauls proclaim they are all descended, as Caesar writes?
derivation: Iconic claim of Gallic descent. Anchored to the Gauls; single divine-name answer supported verbatim (ab Dite patre prognatos). Direct question with the source's acc.+inf. (se prognatos esse) plus parenthetical attribution.

author: Caesar
source_text: Ob eam causam spatia omnis temporis non numero dierum sed noctium finiunt; dies natales et mensum et annorum initia sic observant ut noctem dies subsequatur.
question: Utrum numero dierum an noctium Galli omnia temporis spatia finire soleant Caesar tradit?
question_en: Does Caesar report that the Gauls reckon all spans of time by the count of days or of nights?
derivation: The well-known Celtic night-reckoning custom. Anchored to the Gauls; disjunctive question with a single verifiable answer supported verbatim (non numero dierum sed noctium). Indirect question (soleant, subj.) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Germani multum ab hac consuetudine differunt. Nam neque druides habent, qui rebus divinis praesint, neque sacrificiis student. Deorum numero eos solos ducunt, quos cernunt et quorum aperte opibus iuvantur, Solem et Vulcanum et Lunam, reliquos ne fama quidem acceperunt.
question: Quos solos deorum numero Germanos ducere Caesar tradit?
question_en: Which gods alone does Caesar report the Germani count among the gods?
answer_en: The Sun, Vulcan, and the Moon.
derivation: Specific German religious custom (contrast with the Gauls). Anchored to the Germani; complete three-name enumeration supported verbatim (Solem et Vulcanum et Lunam). Indirect statement (Germanos ducere) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Agriculturae non student, maiorque pars eorum victus in lacte, caseo, carne consistit.
question: In quibus rebus maiorem partem victus Germanorum consistere Caesar scribit?
question_en: In what does Caesar say the greater part of the Germani's food consists?
derivation: Specific German dietary custom. Anchored to the Germani; complete three-item enumeration supported verbatim (in lacte, caseo, carne consistit). Indirect statement (maiorem partem... consistere) under scribit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Itaque ea quae fertilissima Germaniae sunt loca circum Hercyniam silvam, quam Eratostheni et quibusdam Graecis fama notam esse video, quam illi Orcyniam appellant, Volcae Tectosages occupaverunt atque ibi consederunt.
question: Quam gentem Gallorum loca circum Hercyniam silvam occupavisse Caesar tradit?
question_en: Which Gallic people, according to Caesar, occupied the lands around the Hercynian forest?
derivation: Named-people fact about settlement around the Hercynian forest. Anchored to the Hercynian forest; single people-name answer supported verbatim (Volcae Tectosages occupaverunt). Indirect statement (gentem... occupavisse) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Huius Hercyniae silvae, quae supra demonstrata est, latitudo novem dierum iter expedito patet.
question: Quot dierum iter in latitudinem Hercyniam silvam patere Caesar tradit?
question_en: How many days' journey wide does Caesar report the Hercynian forest to be?
derivation: Measure fact for the Hercynian forest's breadth. Anchored to the Hercynian forest; single number answer supported verbatim (latitudo novem dierum iter ... patet). Indirect statement (silvam patere) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Sunt item, quae appellantur alces. Harum est consimilis capris figura et varietas pellium, sed magnitudine paulo antecedunt mutilaeque sunt cornibus et crura sine nodis articulisque habent neque quietis causa procumbunt.
question: Quas feras Hercyniae silvae crura sine nodis articulisque habere Caesar tradit?
question_en: Which beasts of the Hercynian forest does Caesar report have legs without knots or joints?
derivation: Named animal of the Hercynian forest with its signature feature (jointless legs). Anchored to the forest; single animal-name answer supported verbatim (alces ... crura sine nodis articulisque habent). Indirect statement (feras habere) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Tertium est genus eorum, qui uri appellantur. Hi sunt magnitudine paulo infra elephantos, specie et colore et figura tauri.
question: Quo animali uros magnitudine paulo inferiores esse Caesar scribit?
question_en: To which animal does Caesar report the uri (aurochs) are slightly inferior in size?
answer_en: Elephants (the uri are a little smaller than elephants).
derivation: Named animal of the Hercynian forest with a comparative-size fact. Anchored to the uri; single answer supported verbatim (magnitudine paulo infra elephantos). Indirect statement (uros inferiores esse) under scribit; abl. of comparison.

author: Caesar
source_text: per Arduennam silvam, quae est totius Galliae maxima atque ab ripis Rheni finibusque Treverorum ad Nervios pertinet milibusque amplius quingentis in longitudinem patet
question: Quam silvam totius Galliae maximam esse Caesar tradit?
question_en: Which forest does Caesar report is the largest in all Gaul?
derivation: Superlative geography fact. Anchored to Gaul; single place-name answer supported verbatim (quae est totius Galliae maxima). Indirect statement (silvam... esse) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Catuvolcus, rex dimidiae partis Eburonum, qui una cum Ambiorige consilium inierat, aetate iam confectus, cum laborem aut belli aut fugae ferre non posset, omnibus precibus detestatus Ambiorigem, qui eius consilii auctor fuisset, taxo, cuius magna in Gallia Germaniaque copia est, se exanimavit.
question: Qua re Catuvolcus, dimidiae partis Eburonum rex, se exanimaverit Caesar tradit?
question_en: With what did Catuvolcus, king of half the Eburones, kill himself, according to Caesar?
derivation: Named-person fact: the manner of Catuvolcus' suicide. Anchored to Catuvolcus + the Eburones; single answer supported verbatim (taxo ... se exanimavit). Indirect question (exanimaverit, subj.) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Simili ratione ibi Vercingetorix, Celtilli filius, Arvernus, summae potentiae adulescens, cuius pater principatum Galliae totius obtinuerat et ob eam causam, quod regnum appetebat, ab civitate erat interfectus, convocatis suis clientibus facile incendit.
question: Cuius gentis fuit Vercingetorix, dux Gallorum, secundum Caesarem?
question_en: Of what people was Vercingetorix, the leader of the Gauls, according to Caesar?
derivation: Name/ethnicity fact for the central figure of Book 7. Anchored to Vercingetorix; predicate 'Arvernus' supported verbatim. Vercingetorix the Arvernian is closed-book staple history; single short answer.

author: Caesar
source_text: Simili ratione ibi Vercingetorix, Celtilli filius, Arvernus, summae potentiae adulescens, cuius pater principatum Galliae totius obtinuerat et ob eam causam, quod regnum appetebat, ab civitate erat interfectus, convocatis suis clientibus facile incendit.
question: Cuius filius fuit Vercingetorix Arvernus?
question_en: Whose son was Vercingetorix the Arvernian?
derivation: Relation fact anchored to Vercingetorix; single named answer 'Celtilli' supported verbatim by 'Celtilli filius'. The father Celtillus (who sought kingship and was killed) is a fixed genealogical fact; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Totius Galliae concilium Bibracte indicitur. Eodem conveniunt undique frequentes. Multitudinis suffragiis res permittitur: ad unum omnes Vercingetorigem probant imperatorem.
question: Quem totius Galliae concilium Bibracte habitum imperatorem belli ad unum probavit?
question_en: Whom did the council of all Gaul held at Bibracte unanimously approve as commander of the war?
derivation: Office/election fact anchored to the council at Bibracte; single named answer supported verbatim by 'ad unum omnes Vercingetorigem probant imperatorem'. The choice of Vercingetorix as leader of the revolt is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Vbi ea dies venit, Carnutes Cotuato et Conconnetodumno ducibus, desperatis hominibus, Cenabum signo dato concurrunt civesque Romanos, qui negotiandi causa ibi constiterant, in his Gaium Fufium Citam, honestum equitem Romanum, qui rei frumentariae iussu Caesaris praeerat, interficiunt bonaque eorum diripiunt.
question: In quo oppido Carnutes, caede civium Romanorum facta, Gallici belli initium fecerunt?
question_en: In what town did the Carnutes, by massacring Roman citizens, make the beginning of the Gallic war?
derivation: Place fact anchored to the Carnutes; single town answer supported verbatim by 'Carnutes ... Cenabum ... civesque Romanos ... interficiunt'. The massacre at Cenabum, the spark of the revolt, is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Caesar ad oppidum Avaricum, quod erat maximum munitissimumque in finibus Biturigum atque agri fertilissima regione, profectus est, quod eo oppido recepto civitatem Biturigum se in potestatem redacturum confidebat.
question: Quod oppidum maximum munitissimumque in finibus Biturigum fuisse Caesar scribit?
question_en: Which town does Caesar write was the largest and most fortified in the territory of the Bituriges?
derivation: Place fact anchored to the Bituriges and Caesar; single town answer supported verbatim by 'Avaricum, quod erat maximum munitissimumque in finibus Biturigum'. Indirect statement (fuisse) under scribit; the storming of Avaricum is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Denique ex omni numero, qui fuit circiter milium XL, vix DCCC, qui primo clamore audito se ex oppido eiecerunt, incolumes ad Vercingetorigem pervenerunt.
question: Cum Avaricum a Romanis expugnatum esset, ex circiter quadraginta milibus hominum quot vix incolumes ad Vercingetorigem pervenerunt?
question_en: When Avaricum was stormed by the Romans, out of about forty thousand people how many scarcely reached Vercingetorix safely?
derivation: Number fact anchored to Avaricum and Vercingetorix; the count (vix DCCC out of circiter milium XL) supported verbatim. The slaughter at Avaricum, with barely 800 of 40,000 surviving, is the iconic figure Caesar gives; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Omnium consensu hac sententia probata uno die amplius XX urbes Biturigum incenduntur.
question: Quot urbes Biturigum uno die, Vercingetorige suadente, a Gallis incensae sunt?
question_en: How many towns of the Bituriges were burned by the Gauls in one day, on Vercingetorix's plan?
derivation: Number fact anchored to the Bituriges and Vercingetorix's scorched-earth policy; answer 'amplius XX' supported verbatim. Distinctive count; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Exercitum in duas partes divisit: quattuor legiones in Senones Parisiosque Labieno ducendas dedit, sex ipse in Arvernos ad oppidum Gergoviam secundum flumen Elaver duxit.
question: Ad quod Arvernorum oppidum Caesar sex legiones secundum flumen Elaver duxit?
question_en: To which town of the Arverni did Caesar lead six legions along the river Elaver (Allier)?
derivation: Place fact anchored to the Arverni, Caesar, six legions and the Elaver; single town answer supported verbatim by 'sex ipse in Arvernos ad oppidum Gergoviam secundum flumen Elaver duxit'. Gergovia, the Arvernian stronghold, is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Nostri, cum undique premerentur, XLVI centurionibus amissis deiecti sunt loco.
question: Quot centuriones Caesaris in proelio ad Gergoviam adverso amissi sunt?
question_en: How many of Caesar's centurions were lost in the unsuccessful battle at Gergovia?
derivation: Number fact anchored to the repulse at Gergovia; answer (XLVI = 46) supported verbatim by 'XLVI centurionibus amissis'. The loss of officers at Gergovia is the distinctive figure of Caesar's one defeat in the campaign; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Fugato omni equitatu Vercingetorix copias, ut pro castris collocaverat, reduxit protinusque Alesiam, quod est oppidum Mandubiorum, iter facere coepit.
question: Cuius gentis oppidum erat Alesia, quo Vercingetorix victus se recepit?
question_en: Of what people was Alesia the town, to which Vercingetorix withdrew after defeat?
derivation: Place fact anchored to Alesia and Vercingetorix; single answer supported verbatim by 'Alesiam, quod est oppidum Mandubiorum'. Alesia of the Mandubii, site of the final siege, is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Coactis equitum VIII milibus et peditum circiter CCL haec in Aeduorum finibus recensebantur, numerusque inibatur, praefecti constituebantur.
question: Quantae copiae equitum peditumque coactae sunt, ut Gallis Alesiae obsessis subsidio venirent?
answer: Octo milia equitum et circiter ducenta quinquaginta milia peditum.
question_en: How large a force of cavalry and infantry was raised to relieve the Gauls besieged at Alesia?
answer_en: Eight thousand cavalry and about two hundred fifty thousand infantry.
derivation: Number fact anchored to the relief army for Alesia; counts (VIII milibus equitum, circiter CCL [milia] peditum) supported verbatim. The size of the Gallic relief army is the iconic figure of the siege; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Commio Atrebati, Viridomaro et Eporedorigi Aeduis, Vercassivellauno Arverno, consobrino Vercingetorigis, summa imperi traditur.
question: Quis Arvernus, Vercingetorigis consobrinus, inter quattuor duces auxiliaribus copiis ad Alesiam praefuit?
question_en: Which Arvernian, cousin of Vercingetorix, was among the four leaders set over the relief forces at Alesia?
derivation: Name/relation fact anchored to the relief army and to Vercingetorix; single named answer supported verbatim by 'Vercassivellauno Arverno, consobrino Vercingetorigis'. Anchored as the Arvernian cousin to give a single referent among the four joint commanders; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Quod si indiligentiores fuerint, milia hominum delecta octoginta una secum interitura demonstrat.
question: Quot milia hominum delecta una cum Vercingetorige Alesiae obsidebantur?
question_en: How many thousand chosen men were besieged at Alesia together with Vercingetorix?
derivation: Number fact anchored to Vercingetorix and Alesia; answer 'octoginta milia' supported verbatim ('milia hominum delecta octoginta una secum interitura'), echoed by Critognatus' 'hominum milibus LXXX' (7.77). Closed-book count of the Alesia garrison.

author: Caesar
source_text: Mittuntur de his rebus ad Caesarem legati. Iubet arma tradi, principes produci. Ipse in munitione pro castris consedit: eo duces producuntur; Vercingetorix deditur, arma proiciuntur.
question: Quis dux Gallorum post Alesiae obsidionem Caesari deditus est, armis proiectis?
question_en: Which leader of the Gauls was surrendered to Caesar after the siege of Alesia, his arms thrown down?
derivation: Event fact anchored to Alesia and Caesar; single named answer supported verbatim by 'Vercingetorix deditur, arma proiciuntur'. The surrender of Vercingetorix at Alesia is among the most famous events in Roman history; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Labienus eo supplemento, quod nuper ex Italia venerat, relicto Agedinci, ut esset impedimentis praesidio, cum quattuor legionibus Lutetiam proficiscitur. Id est oppidum Parisiorum, quod positum est in insula fluminis Sequanae.
question: Cuius gentis oppidum erat Lutetia, in insula fluminis Sequanae positum, quod Labienus petivit?
question_en: Of what people was Lutetia the town, set on an island of the river Sequana (Seine), to which Labienus marched?
derivation: Place fact anchored to Lutetia, the Seine, and Labienus; single answer supported verbatim by 'Lutetiam ... Id est oppidum Parisiorum, quod positum est in insula fluminis Sequanae'. Lutetia of the Parisii (Paris) is closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: His litteris cognitis Romae dierum viginti supplicatio redditur.
question: Quot dierum supplicatio Romae decreta est, cum de Caesaris rebus ad Alesiam gestis cognitum esset?
question_en: A thanksgiving of how many days was decreed at Rome when Caesar's deeds at Alesia became known?
derivation: Number fact anchored to Rome and the close of the Alesia campaign; answer 'viginti dierum' supported verbatim by 'dierum viginti supplicatio redditur'. The twenty-day thanksgiving is the iconic closing fact of Book 7; closed-book.

author: Cato
source_text: Et virum bonum quom laudabant, ita laudabant: bonum agricolam bonumque colonum; amplissime laudari existimabatur qui ita laudabatur.
question: Quibus verbis maiores, ut Cato scribit, virum bonum amplissime laudabant?
question_en: With what words, as Cato writes, did the ancestors most highly praise a good man?
answer_en: A good farmer and a good husbandman.
derivation: The famous claim of the praefatio: the highest praise for a man was to call him 'bonum agricolam bonumque colonum.' Anchored to Cato + the maiores; the answer is the exact predicate phrase, supported verbatim. Closed-book: one of the most-quoted lines of Cato. Imperfect 'laudabant' kept indicative; 'ut Cato scribit' is a parenthetical author-frame.

author: Cato
source_text: At ex agricolis et viri fortissimi et milites strenuissimi gignuntur, maximeque pius quaestus stabilissimusque consequitur minimeque invidiosus, minimeque male cogitantes sunt qui in eo studio occupati sunt.
question: Ex quibus hominibus et viros fortissimos et milites strenuissimos gigni Cato adfirmat?
question_en: From which men does Cato assert that both the bravest men and the most vigorous soldiers are born?
derivation: Cato's celebrated claim that farmers are the source of the bravest men and most vigorous soldiers. Anchored to Cato + agricolae; single answer 'ex agricolis,' supported verbatim. Closed-book and widely quoted. Indirect statement: passive infinitive 'gigni' with accusative subjects under 'adfirmat.'

author: Cato
source_text: Maiores nostri sic habuerunt et ita in legibus posiverunt: furem dupli condemnari, foeneratorem quadrupli.
question: Quanti, ut Cato refert, maiores in legibus foeneratorem condemnari iusserunt?
question_en: For how much, as Cato reports, did the ancestors order in their laws that a usurer be condemned?
derivation: Preface's comparison: the laws condemned a thief to double, a usurer to quadruple — Cato's point that usury was judged worse than theft. Anchored to Cato + the maiores' laws; genitive-of-penalty answer 'quadrupli' supported verbatim ('foeneratorem quadrupli'). Closed-book datum on Roman attitudes to usury. 'condemnari' passive inf. with acc. subject under 'iusserunt.'

author: Cato
source_text: Praedium quod primum siet, si me rogabis, sic dicam: de omnibus agris optimoque loco iugera agri centum, vinea est prima, vel si vino multo est; secundo loco hortus irriguus; tertio salictum; quarto oletum; quinto pratum; sexto campus frumentarius; septimo silva caedua; octavo arbustum; nono glandaria silva.
question: Quod agri genus Cato inter omnia primo loco numerat?
question_en: Which kind of farmland does Cato rank first among all?
derivation: Cato's well-known ranking of the nine kinds of farmland, with the vineyard (vinea) first. Anchored to Cato; single answer 'vineam,' supported verbatim by 'vinea est prima.' Closed-book: a standard datum in discussions of Roman agronomy. Only the first place is asked (the full list would fail short-answer).

author: Cato
source_text: Quid est agrum bene colere? Bene arare. Quid secundum? Arare. Quid tertium? Stercorare.
question: Quid Cato primum esse dicit in agro bene colendo?
question_en: What does Cato say is the first thing in cultivating a field well?
derivation: Cato's celebrated catechism on good husbandry: first to plow well, second to plow, third to manure ('arare, arare, stercorare'). Anchored to Cato; single answer 'bene arare,' supported verbatim. Closed-book: among the most-quoted lines of Cato. Indirect statement under 'dicit.'

author: Cato
source_text: Brassica est quae omnibus holeribus antistat.
question: Quod holus Cato omnibus holeribus antistare scribit?
question_en: Which vegetable does Cato write surpasses all other vegetables?
derivation: Cato's famous superlative praise of the cabbage as the best of all vegetables, opening his cabbage-chapter. Anchored to Cato; single answer 'brassicam,' supported verbatim. Closed-book: Cato's enthusiasm for cabbage is well-known trivia (discussed e.g. by Pliny). 'antistare' + dative; acc. subject 'brassicam' under 'scribit.'

author: Gaius
source_text: Nam quod quisque populus ipse sibi ius constituit, id ipsius proprium est vocaturque ius civile, quasi ius proprium civitatis.
question: Quo nomine Gaius id ius appellat, quod quisque populus ipse sibi constituit?
question_en: By what name does Gaius call the law that each people establishes for itself?
derivation: The famous opening definition of ius civile in Gaius's Institutes: the law a people makes for itself is its own and is called ius civile. Closed-book foundational maxim, anchored to Gaius, single named-term answer present verbatim ('vocaturque ius civile').

author: Gaius
source_text: Quod vero naturalis ratio inter omnes homines constituit, id apud omnes populos peraeque custoditur vocaturque ius gentium, quasi quo iure omnes gentes utuntur.
question: Quo nomine Gaius id ius appellat, quod naturalis ratio inter omnes homines constituit?
question_en: By what name does Gaius call the law that natural reason has established among all men?
derivation: Gaius's paired definition: what natural reason establishes among all men is called ius gentium. Closed-book foundational maxim, anchored to Gaius, single named-term answer verbatim ('vocaturque ius gentium').

author: Gaius
source_text: Constant autem iura populi Romani ex legibus, plebiscitis, senatus consultis, constitutionibus principum, edictis eorum, qui ius edicendi habent, responsis prudentium.
question: Ex quibus rebus iura populi Romani constare Gaius scribit?
answer: Ex legibus, plebiscitis, senatus consultis, constitutionibus principum, edictis eorum qui ius edicendi habent, et responsis prudentium.
question_en: Of what does Gaius say the law of the Roman people consists?
answer_en: Of statutes, plebiscites, decrees of the senate, enactments of the emperors, edicts of those who have the right to issue edicts, and the responses of the jurists.
derivation: Gaius's canonical enumeration of the sources (fontes) of Roman law. Closed-book, anchored to Gaius, a closed list of named institutions present verbatim; indirect statement (constare) governed by scribit.

author: Gaius
source_text: unde olim patricii dicebant plebiscitis se non teneri, quia sine auctoritate eorum facta essent; sed postea lex Hortensia lata est, qua cautum est, ut plebiscita universum populum tenerent.
question: Qua lege cautum est ut plebiscita universum populum tenerent, ut Gaius tradit?
question_en: By what law was it provided that plebiscites should bind the whole people, as Gaius reports?
derivation: Gaius records the lex Hortensia, which made plebiscites binding on the entire people (patricians included). Closed-book famous legal-history fact, anchored to the named law, single named-entity answer verbatim ('lex Hortensia lata est, qua cautum est...').

author: Gaius
source_text: Omne autem ius, quo utimur, vel ad personas pertinet vel ad res vel ad actiones.
question: Ad quae tria omne ius quo utimur pertinet, ut Gaius initio Institutionum docet?
answer: Ad personas, ad res, ad actiones.
question_en: To which three things does all the law we use pertain, as Gaius teaches at the opening of the Institutes?
answer_en: To persons, to things, and to actions.
derivation: Gaius's tripartite division of all law into personae, res, actiones, the organizing scheme of the Institutes (and quoted later at Dig. 1.5.1). Closed-book, anchored to Gaius, three-part answer verbatim; indirect statement (pertinere) governed by scribit.

author: Gaius
source_text: Et quidem summa divisio de iure personarum haec est, quod omnes homines aut liberi sunt aut servi.
question: Quae est summa divisio de iure personarum secundum Gaium?
answer: Omnes homines aut liberi sunt aut servi.
question_en: What is the chief division in the law of persons according to Gaius?
answer_en: All men are either free or slaves.
derivation: The most famous single sentence of the law of persons: the summa divisio that all men are either free or slaves. Closed-book maxim, anchored to Gaius + ius personarum, short verifiable answer verbatim.

author: Gaius
source_text: Rursus liberorum hominum alii ingenui sunt, alii libertini. Ingenui sunt, qui liberi nati sunt; libertini, qui ex iusta servitute manumissi sunt.
question: In quae duo genera liberos homines Gaius dividit?
question_en: Into which two classes does Gaius divide free men?
derivation: Gaius's subdivision of free men into ingenui (born free) and libertini (manumitted from lawful slavery). Closed-book, anchored to Gaius, two named-term answer verbatim ('alii ingenui sunt, alii libertini').

author: Gaius
source_text: Rursus libertinorum tria sunt genera: Nam aut cives Romani aut Latini aut dediticiorum numero sunt.
question: Quae tria genera libertinorum Gaius distinguit?
question_en: Which three classes of freedmen does Gaius distinguish?
derivation: Gaius's threefold classification of freedmen: cives Romani, Latini (Iuniani), dediticii. Closed-book, anchored to Gaius + libertini, three named-entity answer verbatim ('aut cives Romani aut Latini aut dediticiorum numero sunt').

author: Gaius
source_text: Nam in cuius persona tria haec concurrunt, ut maior sit annorum triginta, et ex iure Quiritium domini, et iusta ac legitima manumissione liberetur, id est vindicta aut censu aut testamento, is civis Romanus fit.
question: Quibus tribus modis iusta ac legitima manumissio fieri potest secundum Gaium?
question_en: By which three modes can a lawful and formal manumission be effected according to Gaius?
answer_en: By the rod (vindicta), by the census, and by will.
derivation: The classic triad of formal manumission: vindicta, censu, testamento. Closed-book, anchored to Gaius + manumissio, three named-mode answer verbatim ('id est vindicta aut censu aut testamento').

author: Gaius
source_text: Quod autem de aetate servi requiritur, lege Aelia Sentia introductum est. Nam ea lex minores XXX annorum servos non aliter voluit manumissos cives Romanos fieri, quam si vindicta, apud consilium iusta causa manumissionis adprobata, liberati fuerint.
question: Servos cuius aetatis lex Aelia Sentia non aliter manumissos cives Romanos fieri voluit quam vindicta, iusta causa probata, ut Gaius scribit?
question_en: Slaves of what age did the lex Aelia Sentia allow to become Roman citizens on manumission only by vindicta, after a just cause had been approved, as Gaius writes?
derivation: Gaius: under the lex Aelia Sentia slaves under 30 could become cives Romani on manumission only by vindicta with a just cause approved before the council. Closed-book numeric/legal fact, anchored to the named law, number answer verbatim ('minores XXX annorum servos').

author: Gaius
source_text: Item in potestate nostra sunt liberi nostri, quos iustis nuptiis procreavimus. Quod ius proprium civium Romanorum est.
question: Quorum hominum proprium esse patriam in liberos potestatem Gaius adfirmat?
question_en: To which men does Gaius affirm that paternal power over children belongs as their own peculiar right?
derivation: Gaius's hallmark claim that patria potestas over legitimate children is a right peculiar to Roman citizens. Closed-book, anchored to Gaius + patria potestas, single named-entity answer verbatim ('Quod ius proprium civium Romanorum est'); indirect statement (proprium esse) governed by adfirmat.

author: Gaius
source_text: Fratris filiam uxorem ducere licet: Idque primum in usum uenit, cum divus Claudius Agrippinam, fratris sui filiam, uxorem duxisset.
question: Quis primus fratris filiam, scilicet Agrippinam, uxorem duxit, unde id in usum venit, ut Gaius refert?
question_en: Who first married his brother's daughter, namely Agrippina, whence the practice came into use, as Gaius reports?
derivation: Gaius records that marrying a brother's daughter first came into use when the emperor Claudius married Agrippina, his brother's daughter. Closed-book historical fact, anchored to Claudius + Agrippina, single named-entity answer verbatim ('cum divus Claudius Agrippinam, fratris sui filiam, uxorem duxisset').

author: Gaius
source_text: Olim itaque tribus modis in manum conveniebant: usu, farreo, coemptione.
question: Quibus tribus modis mulieres olim in manum conveniebant secundum Gaium?
question_en: By which three modes did women formerly pass into marital subordination (manus) according to Gaius?
answer_en: By usage (usu), by the spelt-cake rite (farreo), and by coemptio.
derivation: Gaius's classic triad of the modes of entering manus: usu, farreo, coemptione. Closed-book, anchored to Gaius + manus, three named-mode answer verbatim ('tribus modis in manum conveniebant: usu, farreo, coemptione').

author: Gaius
source_text: Est autem kapitis diminutio prioris status permutatio: Eaque tribus modis accidit: Nam aut maxima est kapitis diminutio aut minor, quam quidam mediam vocant, aut minima.
question: In quot species capitis diminutionem dividi Gaius tradit?
answer: In tres: maximam, minorem sive mediam, et minimam.
question_en: Into how many kinds does Gaius report that capitis diminutio (loss of legal status) is divided?
answer_en: Into three: the greatest (maxima), the lesser or middle (media), and the least (minima).
derivation: Gaius's threefold division of capitis diminutio into maxima, minor (media), and minima. Closed-book legal-doctrine fact with a determinate count, anchored to Gaius + capitis diminutio, three-part answer verbatim ('tribus modis accidit: ... maxima ... minor, quam quidam mediam vocant ... minima').

author: Gaius
source_text: Summa itaque rerum diuisio in duos articulos diducitur: nam aliae sunt diuini iuris, aliae humani.
question: Quae est summa rerum divisio secundum Gaium?
answer: Res aliae divini iuris sunt, aliae humani.
question_en: What is the highest division of things according to Gaius?
answer_en: Some things are of divine law, others of human law.
derivation: Gaius's famous summa divisio rerum opening the law of things: things are either divini iuris or humani iuris. Closed-book foundational maxim, anchored to Gaius + ius rerum, short two-part answer present verbatim ('aliae sunt diuini iuris, aliae humani'); parallels the Book I summa divisio of persons.

author: Gaius
source_text: Diuini iuris sunt ueluti res sacrae et religiosae.
question: Quae sunt res divini iuris secundum Gaium?
question_en: What are the things of divine law according to Gaius?
answer_en: Sacred things (res sacrae) and religious things (res religiosae).
derivation: Gaius subdivides res divini iuris into res sacrae and res religiosae. Closed-book canonical division, anchored to Gaius + res divini iuris, two named-term answer present verbatim ('res sacrae et religiosae').

author: Gaius
source_text: Sacrae sunt, quae diis superis consecratae sunt; religiosae, quae diis Manibus relictae sunt.
question: Quibus diis res sacrae consecratae et res religiosae relictae sunt secundum Gaium?
answer: Sacrae diis superis, religiosae diis Manibus.
question_en: To which gods are sacred things consecrated and religious things left, according to Gaius?
answer_en: Sacred things to the gods above (dii superi), religious things to the gods of the dead (dii Manes).
derivation: Gaius's defining distinction between res sacrae (consecrated to the gods above) and res religiosae (left to the di Manes). Closed-book definitional fact, anchored to Gaius, paired named-entity answer present verbatim ('quae diis superis consecratae sunt ... quae diis Manibus relictae sunt').

author: Gaius
source_text: Hae autem res, quae humani iuris sunt, aut publicae sunt aut priuatae.
question: In quae duo genera res humani iuris dividi Gaius tradit?
question_en: Into which two kinds does Gaius report that things of human law are divided?
derivation: Gaius's subdivision of res humani iuris into res publicae and res privatae. Closed-book canonical division, anchored to Gaius + res humani iuris, two-part answer present verbatim ('aut publicae sunt aut priuatae'); indirect statement (res dividi) governed by tradit.

author: Gaius
source_text: Corporales hae sunt, quae tangi possunt, uelut fundus, homo, uestis, aurum, argentum et denique aliae res innumerabiles.
question: Quas res Gaius corporales esse dicit?
question_en: Which things does Gaius say are corporeal?
derivation: Gaius's classic definition of res corporales as things that can be touched (opposed to res incorporales). Closed-book jurisprudential definition, anchored to Gaius, short answer present verbatim ('Corporales hae sunt, quae tangi possunt'); indirect statement (res corporales esse) governed by dicit.

author: Gaius
source_text: Res praeterea aut mancipi sunt aut nec mancipi.
question: In quae duo genera res praeterea dividi Gaius scribit?
answer: In res mancipi et nec mancipi.
question_en: Into which two kinds does Gaius write that things are further divided?
answer_en: Into things mancipi and things nec mancipi.
derivation: Gaius's famous division of things into res mancipi and res nec mancipi, fundamental to Roman property law. Closed-book canonical division, anchored to Gaius, two named-term answer present verbatim ('aut mancipi sunt aut nec mancipi').

author: Gaius
source_text: Sed item fere omnia, quae incorporalia sunt, nec mancipi sunt, exceptis seruitutibus praediorum rusticorum; nam eas mancipi esse constat, quamuis sint ex numero rerum incorporalium.
question: Quae sola ex rebus incorporalibus res mancipi esse Gaius adfirmat?
question_en: Which incorporeal things alone does Gaius affirm to be res mancipi?
derivation: Gaius notes that although nearly all incorporeal things are nec mancipi, rustic praedial servitudes are res mancipi (an instance of the classic res mancipi set). Closed-book, anchored to Gaius, single named-entity answer present verbatim ('exceptis seruitutibus praediorum rusticorum; nam eas mancipi esse constat'); indirect statement (servitutes mancipi esse) governed by adfirmat.

author: Gaius
source_text: Vsucapio autem mobilium quidem rerum anno completur, fundi uero et aedium biennio; et ita lege XII tabularum cautum est.
question: Quibus temporibus usucapionem rerum mobilium et fundi compleri Gaius scribit?
question_en: In what periods does Gaius write that usucapion of movable things and of land is completed?
answer_en: Of movables in one year, of land in two years.
derivation: Gaius gives the usucapio periods fixed by the Twelve Tables: one year for movables, two years for land and buildings. Closed-book crisp numeric fact, anchored to Gaius + XII Tables, both periods present verbatim ('mobilium quidem rerum anno completur, fundi uero et aedium biennio'); indirect statement (usucapionem compleri) governed by scribit.

author: Gaius
source_text: Praeterea id, quod in solo nostro ab aliquo aedificatum est, quamuis ille suo nomine aedificauerit, iure naturali nostrum fit, quia superficies solo cedit.
question: Quo principio id quod in solo nostro ab alio aedificatum est nostrum fieri Gaius docet?
question_en: On what principle does Gaius teach that what another builds on our land becomes ours?
answer_en: Because the surface yields to the soil (superficies solo cedit).
derivation: Gaius states the famous maxim superficies solo cedit: what is built on our soil becomes ours by natural law. Closed-book classical legal maxim, anchored to Gaius, short answer present verbatim ('quia superficies solo cedit'); indirect statement (id nostrum fieri) governed by docet.

author: Gaius
source_text: Testamentorum autem genera initio duo fuerunt: nam aut calatis comitiis testamentum faciebant, quae comitia bis in anno testamentis faciendis destinata erant, aut in procinctu, id est, cum belli causa arma sumebant: procinctus est enim expeditus et armatus exercitus. Accessit deinde tertium genus testamenti, quod per aes et libram agitur.
question: Quae tria genera testamentorum apud Romanos fuisse Gaius commemorat?
answer: Calatis comitiis, in procinctu, et per aes et libram.
question_en: Which three kinds of testament does Gaius record existed among the Romans?
answer_en: In the calate assembly (calatis comitiis), in battle array (in procinctu), and by bronze and balance (per aes et libram).
derivation: Gaius enumerates the three historical forms of testament: the two original ones (calatis comitiis and in procinctu) and the later per aes et libram. Closed-book famous legal-history fact, anchored to Gaius, three named forms present verbatim across 2.101-102; indirect statement (genera fuisse) governed by commemorat.

author: Gaius
source_text: Heredes autem aut necessarii dicuntur aut sui et necessarii aut extranei.
question: In quae tria genera heredes dividi Gaius scribit?
answer: In necessarios, suos et necessarios, et extraneos.
question_en: Into which three classes does Gaius write that heirs are divided?
answer_en: Into necessary heirs (necessarii), own-and-necessary heirs (sui et necessarii), and external heirs (extranei).
derivation: Gaius's threefold classification of heirs: necessarii, sui et necessarii, extranei. Closed-book canonical division, anchored to Gaius, three named-term answer present verbatim ('aut necessarii ... aut sui et necessarii aut extranei'); indirect statement (heredes dividi) governed by scribit.

author: Gaius
source_text: Legatorum itaque genera sunt quattuor: aut enim per uindicationem legamus aut per damnationem aut sinendi modo aut per praeceptionem.
question: Quot sunt legatorum genera secundum Gaium, et quae?
answer: Quattuor: per vindicationem, per damnationem, sinendi modo, et per praeceptionem.
question_en: How many kinds of legacy are there according to Gaius, and which?
answer_en: Four: by vindication (per vindicationem), by condemnation (per damnationem), by permission (sinendi modo), and by preception (per praeceptionem).
derivation: Gaius's classic fourfold division of legacies with the determinate count. Closed-book canonical division, anchored to Gaius, count and four named kinds present verbatim ('genera sunt quattuor: aut enim per uindicationem ... aut per damnationem aut sinendi modo aut per praeceptionem').

author: Gaius
source_text: Lata est itaque lex Falcidia, qua cautum est, ne plus ei legare liceat quam dodrantem: itaque necesse est, ut heres quartam partem hereditatis habeat.
question: Quam partem hereditatis heredi servari lex Falcidia iubet, ut Gaius scribit?
question_en: What portion of the inheritance does the lex Falcidia require to be reserved for the heir, as Gaius writes?
derivation: Gaius records that the lex Falcidia capped legacies at three-quarters (dodrans), guaranteeing the heir a quarter (the Falcidian quarter). Closed-book famous numeric/legal fact, anchored to the named lex Falcidia + Gaius, fraction answer present verbatim ('necesse est, ut heres quartam partem hereditatis habeat').

author: Gaius
source_text: Nunc transeamus ad obligationes, quarum summa diuisio in duas species diducitur: omnis enim obligatio uel ex contractu nascitur uel ex delicto.
question: Ex quibus duabus rebus omnem obligationem nasci Gaius scribit?
answer: Vel ex contractu uel ex delicto.
question_en: From which two sources does Gaius write that every obligation arises?
answer_en: Either from contract or from delict.
derivation: Gaius's famous summa divisio of obligations: every obligation arises either ex contractu or ex delicto. Closed-book foundational maxim of Roman law, anchored to Gaius, two-part answer present verbatim ('omnis enim obligatio uel ex contractu nascitur uel ex delicto'); indirect statement (obligationem nasci) governed by scribit.

author: Gaius
source_text: Et prius uideamus de his, quae ex contractu nascuntur. harum autem quattuor genera sunt: aut enim re contrahitur obligatio aut uerbis aut litteris aut consensu.
question: Quot sunt genera obligationum quae ex contractu nascuntur secundum Gaium, et quibus modis?
question_en: How many kinds of contractual obligation are there according to Gaius, and by what means?
answer_en: Four: by thing (re), by words, by writing, and by consent.
derivation: Gaius's fourfold classification of contractual obligations (re, verbis, litteris, consensu) with the determinate count of four. Closed-book canonical division, anchored to Gaius, count and named modes verbatim ('quattuor genera sunt: aut enim re ... aut uerbis aut litteris aut consensu').

author: Gaius
source_text: Consensu fiunt obligationes in emptionibus et uenditionibus, locationibus conductionibus, societatibus, mandatis.
question: In quibus quattuor contractibus consensu obligationes fieri Gaius docet?
answer: In emptione uenditione, locatione conductione, societate, mandato.
question_en: In which four contracts does Gaius teach that obligations arise by consent?
answer_en: In sale (emptio venditio), hire (locatio conductio), partnership (societas), and mandate (mandatum).
derivation: Gaius's list of the four consensual contracts. Closed-book canonical enumeration, anchored to Gaius, the four named contracts present verbatim ('in emptionibus et uenditionibus, locationibus conductionibus, societatibus, mandatis'); indirect statement (obligationes fieri) governed by docet.

author: Gaius
source_text: Transeamus nunc ad obligationes, quae ex delicto nascuntur, ueluti si quis furtum fecerit, bona rapuerit, damnum dederit, iniuriam commiserit.
question: Quae quattuor delicta Gaius commemorat, ex quibus obligationes ex delicto nascuntur?
question_en: Which four wrongs does Gaius mention as giving rise to obligations from delict?
answer_en: Theft, robbery, wrongful damage, and outrage (furtum, rapina, damnum, iniuria).
derivation: Gaius's enumeration of the delicts that produce obligations: theft (furtum fecerit), robbery (bona rapuerit), wrongful damage (damnum dederit), and outrage (iniuriam commiserit). Closed-book named division of the law of delicts, anchored to Gaius, four named delicts present in substance verbatim.

author: Gaius
source_text: Furtorum autem genera Ser. Sulpicius et Masurius Sabinus IIII esse dixerunt, manifestum et nec manifestum, conceptum et oblatum.
question: Quot genera furtorum Seruius Sulpicius et Masurius Sabinus esse dixerunt, ut Gaius refert?
answer: Quattuor: manifestum, nec manifestum, conceptum, oblatum.
question_en: How many kinds of theft did Servius Sulpicius and Masurius Sabinus say there were, as Gaius reports?
answer_en: Four: manifest, non-manifest, conceptum (theft discovered on a search), and oblatum (planted stolen goods).
derivation: Gaius reports that Servius Sulpicius and Masurius Sabinus recognized four genera of theft. Closed-book named division with a determinate count, anchored to the named jurists (and Gaius), count and four named kinds present verbatim ('IIII esse dixerunt, manifestum et nec manifestum, conceptum et oblatum').

author: Gaius
source_text: Furtorum autem genera Ser. Sulpicius et Masurius Sabinus IIII esse dixerunt, manifestum et nec manifestum, conceptum et oblatum; Labeo duo, manifestum et nec manifestum.
question: Quot genera furtorum Labeo esse dixit, ut Gaius refert?
question_en: How many kinds of theft did Labeo say there were, as Gaius reports?
derivation: Gaius records the jurisprudential dispute: against the Sabinian four, Labeo held there were only two genera of theft (manifestum and nec manifestum), treating conceptum and oblatum as species of action. Closed-book, anchored to Labeo (and Gaius), count and named kinds verbatim ('Labeo duo, manifestum et nec manifestum').

author: Gaius
source_text: Damni iniuriae actio constituitur per legem Aquiliam, cuius primo capite cautum est, ut si quis hominem alienum alienamue quadrupedem, quae pecudum numero sit, iniuria occiderit, quanti ea res in eo anno plurimi fuerit, tantum domino dare damnetur.
question: Qua lege actio damni iniuriae constituitur secundum Gaium?
question_en: By what statute is the action for wrongful damage (damnum iniuria datum) established according to Gaius?
derivation: Gaius: the action for damnum iniuria datum is established by the lex Aquilia. Closed-book famous legal fact pairing the named statute with its subject matter, anchored to the lex Aquilia + Gaius, single named-entity answer present verbatim ('Damni iniuriae actio constituitur per legem Aquiliam').

author: Gaius
source_text: Intestatorum hereditates ex lege XII tabularum primum ad suos heredes pertinent.
question: Ad quos primum intestatorum hereditates ex lege XII tabularum pertinere Gaius scribit?
question_en: To whom does Gaius say the inheritances of the intestate first belong under the Twelve Tables?
answer_en: To the sui heredes (the deceased's own heirs).
derivation: Gaius states that under the XII Tables the estate of an intestate first passes to the sui heredes (the first-called class). Closed-book famous rule on the order of intestate succession, anchored to the XII Tables + Gaius, single answer verbatim ('primum ad suos heredes pertinent'); indirect statement (hereditates pertinere) governed by scribit.

author: Gaius
source_text: Si nullus sit suorum heredum, tunc hereditas pertinet ex eadem lege XII tabularum ad adgnatos.
question: Si nullus sit suus heres, ad quos hereditas intestati ex lege XII tabularum pertineat secundum Gaium?
question_en: If there is no suus heres, to whom does the intestate's inheritance pass under the Twelve Tables according to Gaius?
derivation: Gaius gives the second class in the order of intestate succession: failing sui heredes, the estate goes to the agnati. Closed-book famous rule, anchored to the XII Tables + Gaius, single named-class answer verbatim ('Si nullus sit suorum heredum ... ad adgnatos').

author: Gaius
source_text: Si nullus agnatus sit, eadem lex XII tabularum gentiles ad hereditatem uocat.
question: Nullo agnato superstite, quos lex XII tabularum ad hereditatem uocat, ut Gaius refert?
question_en: When no agnate survives, whom do the Twelve Tables call to the inheritance, as Gaius reports?
derivation: Gaius gives the third class in the order of intestate succession: failing agnates, the XII Tables call the gentiles. Closed-book famous rule, anchored to the XII Tables + Gaius, single named-class answer verbatim ('Si nullus agnatus sit ... gentiles ad hereditatem uocat').

author: Gaius
source_text: Verbis obligatio fit ex interrogatione et responsione.
question: Quomodo obligatio uerbis contrahitur secundum Gaium?
question_en: How is a verbal obligation contracted according to Gaius?
derivation: Gaius's definition of the verbal contract (stipulatio): an obligation by words arises from question and answer. Closed-book definitional fact, anchored to Gaius, short phrase answer present verbatim ('Verbis obligatio fit ex interrogatione et responsione').

author: Gaius
source_text: Poena autem iniuriarum ex lege XII tabularum propter membrum quidem ruptum talio erat.
question: Quam poenam lex XII tabularum propter membrum ruptum in iniuriis statuit, ut Gaius tradit?
question_en: What penalty did the Twelve Tables impose for a maimed limb (membrum ruptum) in cases of outrage, as Gaius reports?
derivation: Gaius records the archaic XII Tables penalty for iniuria in the case of a maimed limb: talio (retaliation in kind), the famous lex talionis. Closed-book legal-history fact, anchored to the XII Tables + Gaius, single named-term answer verbatim ('propter membrum quidem ruptum talio erat').

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Iuri operam daturum prius nosse oportet, unde nomen iuris descendat. est autem a iustitia appellatum: nam, ut eleganter celsus definit, ius est ars boni et aequi.
question: Quibus verbis Celsus, ut Ulpianus refert, ius definit?
answer: Ius est ars boni et aequi.
question_en: In what words does Celsus, as Ulpian reports, define law (ius)?
answer_en: Law is the art of the good and the equitable.
derivation: The single most-quoted definition of ius in Roman law, attributed by Ulpian to Celsus. Closed-book famous maxim, entity-anchored to Celsus, short verifiable answer present verbatim ('ius est ars boni et aequi').

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Ius naturale est, quod natura omnia animalia docuit: nam ius istud non humani generis proprium, sed omnium animalium, quae in terra, quae in mari nascuntur, avium quoque commune est.
question: Quomodo Ulpianus ius naturale definit?
question_en: How does Ulpian define natural law (ius naturale)?
answer_en: That which nature has taught all animals.
derivation: Ulpian's famous definition of ius naturale as the law nature taught all animals, not only mankind. Closed-book maxim, anchored to Ulpian + ius naturale, short answer verbatim from the source.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: et cum uno naturali nomine homines appellaremur, iure gentium tria genera esse coeperunt: liberi et his contrarium servi et tertium genus liberti, id est hi qui desierant esse servi.
question: Quae tria genera hominum iure gentium orta esse Ulpianus scribit?
question_en: Which three classes of men does Ulpian say arose by the law of nations (ius gentium)?
derivation: Ulpian: under ius gentium three classes of men arose — liberi, servi, liberti. Closed-book, anchored to Ulpian + ius gentium, three named-entity answer verbatim. Indirect statement (orta esse) governed by scribit.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Ius praetorium est, quod praetores introduxerunt adiuvandi vel supplendi vel corrigendi iuris civilis gratia propter utilitatem publicam. quod et honorarium dicitur ad honorem praetorum sic nominatum.
question: Cuius rei gratia praetores ius praetorium introduxisse Papinianus scribit?
answer: Adiuvandi vel supplendi vel corrigendi iuris civilis gratia.
question_en: For what purpose does Papinian say the praetors introduced praetorian law?
answer_en: For the sake of aiding, supplementing, or correcting the civil law.
derivation: Papinian's classic triad of the purposes of ius praetorium (adiuvandi, supplendi, corrigendi iuris civilis). Closed-book, anchored to Papinian + ius praetorium, answer verbatim. Indirect statement (introduxisse) governed by scribit.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Iustitia est constans et perpetua voluntas ius suum cuique tribuendi.
question: Quomodo Ulpianus iustitiam definit?
answer: Constans et perpetua voluntas ius suum cuique tribuendi.
question_en: How does Ulpian define justice (iustitia)?
answer_en: The constant and perpetual will to render to each his own right.
derivation: The canonical definition of iustitia (later opening Justinian's Institutes), quoted here from Ulpian. Closed-book maxim, anchored to Ulpian + iustitia, short answer verbatim.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Iuris praecepta sunt haec: honeste vivere, alterum non laedere, suum cuique tribuere.
question: Quae sunt tria iuris praecepta secundum Ulpianum?
answer: Honeste vivere, alterum non laedere, suum cuique tribuere.
question_en: What are the three precepts of law according to Ulpian?
answer_en: To live honourably, to harm no one, to render to each his own.
derivation: Ulpian's three iuris praecepta, among the most famous formulas in Western law. Closed-book, anchored to Ulpian + iuris praecepta, three-part answer verbatim.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Postea aucta ad aliquem modum civitate ipsum romulum traditur populum in triginta partes divisisse, quas partes curias appellavit propterea quod tunc reipublicae curam per sententias partium earum expediebat.
question: In quot partes Romulus populum divisisse traditur, quas curias appellavit, ut Pomponius scribit?
question_en: Into how many parts is Romulus said to have divided the people, which he called curiae, as Pomponius writes?
derivation: From Pomponius's history of law: Romulus divided the people into 30 curiae. Closed-book, anchored to Romulus + curiae, single number answer (triginta) verbatim; traditur keeps the 'it is reported' frame (nom.+inf. construction).

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Placuit publica auctoritate decem constitui viros, per quos peterentur leges a graecis civitatibus et civitas fundaretur legibus: quas in tabulas eboreas perscriptas pro rostris composuerunt, ut possint leges apertius percipi. qui ipsi animadverterunt aliquid deesse istis primis legibus ideoque sequenti anno alias duas ad easdem tabulas adiecerunt: et ita ex accedenti appellatae sunt leges duodecim tabularum.
question: Quot viri publica auctoritate constituti sunt, ut leges duodecim tabularum conderentur, secundum Pomponium?
question_en: How many men were appointed by public authority to establish the law of the Twelve Tables, according to Pomponius?
derivation: Pomponius: ten men (decemviri) were appointed and composed the Twelve Tables (two more tables added the following year giving the name). Closed-book, anchored to the Twelve Tables + decemviri, number answer (decem) verbatim from 'decem constitui viros'.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: itaque dictatores proditi sunt, a quibus nec provocandi ius fuit et quibus etiam capitis animadversio data est. hunc magistratum, quoniam summam potestatem habebat, non erat fas ultra sextum mensem retineri.
question: Ultra quot menses dictaturam retineri fas non erat secundum Pomponium?
question_en: Beyond how many months was it not lawful to retain the dictatorship, according to Pomponius?
derivation: Pomponius: the dictatorship, holding supreme power, could not lawfully be held beyond six months. Closed-book institutional fact, anchored to the dictatorship, number answer verbatim ('ultra sextum mensem').

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Post hos fuerunt publius mucius et brutus et manilius, qui fundaverunt ius civile. ex his publius mucius etiam decem libellos reliquit, brutus septem, manilius tres.
question: Qui tres iuris periti ius civile fundavisse a Pomponio dicuntur?
question_en: Which three jurists are said by Pomponius to have founded the civil law?
derivation: Pomponius names the three 'founders of ius civile' (qui fundaverunt ius civile): Publius Mucius Scaevola, Brutus, Manilius. Closed-book in legal history, three named-entity answer verbatim; dicuntur + nom.+inf. (fundavisse).

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Post hos fuit tiberius coruncanius, ut dixi, qui primus profiteri coepit: cuius tamen scriptum nullum exstat, sed responsa complura et memorabilia eius fuerunt.
question: Quis primus ius publice profiteri coepisse a Pomponio traditur?
question_en: Who, according to Pomponius, was the first to begin teaching law publicly?
derivation: Pomponius: Tiberius Coruncanius was the first to teach/give responsa publicly (profiteri). Closed-book historical fact, single named-entity answer, supported by 'qui primus profiteri coepit' (cf. 1.2.2.35 'ante Tiberium Coruncanium publice professum neminem').

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Legis virtus haec est imperare vetare permittere punire.
question: Quae sunt quattuor legis virtutes secundum Modestinum?
question_en: What are the four powers (functions) of law according to Modestinus?
answer_en: To command, to forbid, to permit, to punish.
derivation: Modestinus's four functions of law (imperare, vetare, permittere, punire). Closed-book maxim, anchored to Modestinus + lex, four-part answer verbatim.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
locus: Justinian, Digesta 1.3.31 (Ulpianus 13 ad l. iul. et pap.)
source_text: Princeps legibus solutus est: augusta autem licet legibus soluta non est, principes tamen eadem illi privilegia tribuunt, quae ipsi habent.
question: Quid de principe quoad leges Ulpianus affirmat?
question_en: What does Ulpian assert about the emperor with respect to the laws?
answer_en: That the emperor is freed from (not bound by) the laws.
derivation: The maxim 'princeps legibus solutus est', foundational to later theories of sovereignty, stated here by Ulpian. Closed-book, anchored to Ulpian + princeps, short answer; indirect statement (Principem... solutum esse) governed by affirmat, supported verbatim.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Quod principi placuit, legis habet vigorem: utpote cum lege regia, quae de imperio eius lata est, populus ei et in eum omne suum imperium et potestatem conferat.
question: Quam vim habere id quod principi placuit Ulpianus tradit?
question_en: What force does Ulpian record that whatever pleases the emperor has?
derivation: Ulpian's maxim 'quod principi placuit, legis habet vigorem'. Closed-book, anchored to Ulpian + princeps, short answer 'legis vigorem' verbatim; indirect statement (id... habere) governed by tradit.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Omne ius quo utimur vel ad personas pertinet vel ad res vel ad actiones.
question: Ad quae tria omne ius quo utimur pertinere Gaius scribit?
answer: Ad personas, ad res, ad actiones.
question_en: To which three things does Gaius say that all the law we use pertains?
answer_en: To persons, to things, and to actions.
derivation: Gaius's tripartite division of all law into personae, res, actiones — the organizing scheme of his Institutes. Closed-book, anchored to Gaius, three-part answer verbatim; indirect statement (pertinere) governed by scribit.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: In orbe romano qui sunt ex constitutione imperatoris antonini cives romani effecti sunt.
question: Cuius imperatoris constitutione omnes qui in orbe Romano erant cives Romani facti sunt, ut Ulpianus scribit?
question_en: By the constitution of which emperor did all who were in the Roman world become Roman citizens, as Ulpian writes?
derivation: Ulpian's record of the Constitutio Antoniniana (AD 212), by which Caracalla (Antoninus) granted citizenship to all free inhabitants of the empire. Closed-book famous historical fact, anchored to the emperor Antoninus, single named-entity answer verbatim ('ex constitutione imperatoris Antonini').

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Nihil est aliud hereditas quam successio in universum ius quod defunctus habuit.
question: Quomodo Gaius hereditatem definit?
answer: Successio in universum ius quod defunctus habuit.
question_en: How does Gaius define inheritance (hereditas)?
answer_en: Succession to the entire legal position which the deceased held.
derivation: The classic Roman-law definition of hereditas as universal succession, repeated almost verbatim by Julian at D.50.17.62. Closed-book maxim, anchored to Gaius + hereditas, short answer present verbatim ('successio in universum ius quod defunctus habuit').

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Litus est, quousque maximus fluctus a mari pervenit: idque marcum tullium aiunt, cum arbiter esset, primum constituisse.
question: Quousque litus pertinere Celsus tradit, quam definitionem Marcum Tullium primum constituisse aiunt?
answer: Quousque maximus fluctus a mari pervenit.
question_en: How far does Celsus record that the shore (litus) extends, a definition said to have been first established by Marcus Tullius (Cicero)?
answer_en: As far as the greatest wave reaches from the sea.
derivation: The celebrated juristic definition of litus (the legal boundary of the seashore), which Celsus attributes to Cicero as arbiter. Closed-book, double-anchored (Celsus reporting + Marcus Tullius + litus), short answer verbatim; indirect statement (litus pertinere) governed by tradit.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: hostes hi sunt, qui nobis aut quibus nos publice bellum decrevimus: ceteri latrones aut praedones sunt.
question: Quos Pomponius proprie hostes esse dicit, ceteros latrones aut praedones appellans?
answer: Qui nobis aut quibus nos publice bellum decrevimus.
question_en: Whom does Pomponius say are properly 'enemies' (hostes), calling the rest brigands or robbers?
answer_en: Those on whom, or who on us, we have publicly declared war.
derivation: Pomponius's famous definition distinguishing public enemies (hostes) from mere brigands/pirates (latrones, praedones). Closed-book maxim, anchored to Pomponius + hostes, short answer verbatim; acc.+inf. (quos... hostes esse) governed by dicit.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Mulier autem familiae suae et caput et finis est.
question: Quid mulierem familiae suae esse Ulpianus affirmat?
question_en: What does Ulpian assert a woman is to her own family?
answer_en: Both its head and its end.
derivation: Ulpian's epigrammatic maxim that a woman is both the beginning and the terminus of her own family (she cannot transmit the agnatic line). Closed-book, anchored to Ulpian + mulier/familia, short answer verbatim; acc.+inf. (mulierem... esse) governed by affirmat.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Magna neglegentia culpa est: magna culpa dolus est.
question: Quibus verbis Paulus magnam neglegentiam et magnam culpam definit?
answer: Magna neglegentia culpa est: magna culpa dolus est.
question_en: In what words does Paulus define gross negligence and gross fault?
answer_en: Gross negligence is fault; gross fault is fraud (dolus).
derivation: Paulus's famous gradation equating gross negligence with culpa and gross fault with dolus, foundational to the Roman doctrine of fault. Closed-book maxim, anchored to Paulus, answer verbatim.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Id quod nostrum est sine facto nostro ad alium transferri non potest.
question: Quid de eo quod nostrum est Pomponius regula tradit?
answer: Sine facto nostro ad alium transferri non potest.
question_en: What does Pomponius lay down as a rule about what belongs to us?
answer_en: Without our own act it cannot be transferred to another.
derivation: A celebrated regula iuris on transfer of ownership. Closed-book maxim, anchored to Pomponius, short answer present verbatim.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Quod initio vitiosum est, non potest tractu temporis convalescere.
question: Quid de eo quod initio vitiosum est Paulus regula tradit?
question_en: What does Paulus lay down as a rule about what is defective from the outset?
answer_en: It cannot become valid through the lapse of time.
derivation: The famous maxim that what is void from the beginning cannot be cured by time (cf. D.50.17.210). Closed-book, anchored to Paulus, short answer verbatim.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Nuptias non concubitus, sed consensus facit.
question: Quid nuptias facit, ut Ulpianus regula tradit?
question_en: What makes a marriage, according to Ulpian's rule?
derivation: Ulpian's foundational maxim that consent, not intercourse, constitutes marriage. Closed-book, anchored to Ulpian + nuptiae, short answer supported verbatim ('non concubitus, sed consensus facit').

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Nemo plus iuris ad alium transferre potest, quam ipse haberet.
question: Quantum iuris ad alium quis transferre potest, ut Ulpianus regula tradit?
question_en: How much right can anyone transfer to another, according to Ulpian's rule?
answer_en: No more than he himself would have.
derivation: The single most-cited regula iuris ('no one can transfer more right than he himself has'). Closed-book maxim, anchored to Ulpian, short answer present verbatim.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: In omnibus quidem, maxime tamen in iure aequitas spectanda est.
question: Ubi maxime aequitatem spectandam esse Paulus dicit?
question_en: Where above all does Paulus say equity must be regarded?
derivation: Paulus's famous maxim that equity must be regarded in everything, but most of all in law. Closed-book, anchored to Paulus + aequitas, short answer verbatim; acc.+inf. (aequitatem spectandam esse) governed by dicit.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Non videntur qui errant consentire.
question: Quid de iis qui errant Ulpianus regula tradit?
question_en: What does Ulpian lay down as a rule about those who are in error?
answer_en: They are not regarded as consenting.
derivation: The famous maxim that error excludes consent (the basis of the doctrine of mistake). Closed-book, anchored to Ulpian, short answer present verbatim.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Qui tacet, non utique fatetur: sed tamen verum est eum non negare.
question: Quid de eo qui tacet Paulus regula tradit?
answer: Non utique fatetur, sed tamen verum est eum non negare.
question_en: What does Paulus lay down as a rule about one who keeps silent?
answer_en: He does not necessarily admit, but it is nonetheless true that he does not deny.
derivation: The famous maxim on the legal effect of silence (qui tacet consentire videtur is the later mangling; this is the precise Pauline rule). Closed-book, anchored to Paulus, answer verbatim.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Nemo damnum facit, nisi qui id fecit, quod facere ius non habet.
question: Quem solum damnum facere Paulus regula tradit?
answer: Eum qui id fecit quod facere ius non habet.
question_en: Who alone, by Paulus's rule, does (legally cognizable) damage?
answer_en: He who did what he had no right to do.
derivation: Paulus's famous maxim defining wrongful damage (a cornerstone of the lex Aquilia). Closed-book, anchored to Paulus + damnum, short answer verbatim; acc.+inf. (quem... facere) governed by tradit.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Inpossibilium nulla obligatio est.
question: Quid de impossibilibus quoad obligationem Celsus regula tradit?
question_en: What does Celsus lay down as a rule about impossible things with respect to obligation?
answer_en: There is no obligation to (perform) the impossible.
derivation: Celsus's famous maxim that the impossible binds no one. Closed-book, anchored to Celsus, answer verbatim (note the source spelling 'Inpossibilium').

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Omnis definitio in iure civili periculosa est: parum est enim, ut non subverti posset.
question: Qualem omnem definitionem in iure civili Iavolenus esse pronuntiat?
question_en: What does Javolenus declare every definition in the civil law to be?
derivation: Javolenus's celebrated warning against legal definitions ('every definition in civil law is dangerous'). Closed-book, anchored to Javolenus, short answer verbatim; acc.+inf. (definitionem... esse) governed by pronuntiat.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Iure naturae aequum est neminem cum alterius detrimento et iniuria fieri locupletiorem.
question: Quid iure naturae aequum esse Pomponius tradit de locupletatione cum alterius detrimento?
answer: Neminem cum alterius detrimento et iniuria fieri locupletiorem.
question_en: What does Pomponius hand down as fair by the law of nature regarding enrichment at another's loss?
answer_en: That no one be made richer at another's loss and wrong.
derivation: The foundational maxim against unjust enrichment, the source of the modern principle. Closed-book, anchored to Pomponius, short answer present verbatim; acc.+inf. (neminem... fieri) governed by tradit.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
locus: Justinian, Digesta 50.17.207 (Ulpianus 1 ad l. Iul. et Pap.)
source_text: Res iudicata pro veritate accipitur.
question: Pro qua re rem iudicatam accipi Ulpianus regula tradit?
question_en: As what, by Ulpian's rule, is a matter once adjudged taken?
derivation: The famous maxim that a final judgment is accepted as the truth (basis of res iudicata). Closed-book, anchored to Ulpian, short answer present verbatim; acc.+inf. (rem iudicatam accipi) governed by tradit.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: C. Plinius Traiano imperatori. Tua quidem pietas, imperator sanctissime, optaverat, ut quam tardissime succederes patri; sed di immortales festinaverunt virtutes tuas ad gubernacula rei publicae quam susceperas admovere.
question: Ad quem imperatorem Plinius minor epistulas decimi libri suas direxit, a quo vicissim responsa accepit?
question_en: To which emperor did Pliny the Younger address his letters of the tenth book, and from whom he received replies in turn?
derivation: Addressee fact: the whole of Book X is the official correspondence between Pliny and the emperor Trajan; the salutations read 'C. Plinius Traiano imperatori' / 'Traianus Plinio', and 10.1 addresses Trajan as the new emperor who succeeded his (adoptive) father Nerva. Closed-book famous; entity-anchored to Pliny + Book X; single-name answer.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Rursus, cum transissem in orarias nauculas, contrariis ventis retentus aliquanto tardius quam speraveram, id est XV Kal. Octobres, Bithyniam intravi.
question: In quam provinciam, a Traiano legatus missus, Plinius minor ante diem quintum decimum Kalendas Octobres ingressus est?
question_en: Into which province, sent as Trajan's legate, did Pliny the Younger enter on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October (17 September)?
derivation: Province fact: Pliny governed the province of Bithynia (and Pontus) as Trajan's special legate; he records 'Bithyniam intravi' on a.d. XV Kal. Oct. Answer supported verbatim. Closed-book famous (Pliny's governorship of Bithynia). The full province was Bithynia et Pontus (cf. 10.108 'Bithynas et Ponticas civitates', 10.112 'Bithyni et Pontici').

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Cognitionibus de Christianis interfui numquam: ideo nescio quid et quatenus aut puniri soleat aut quaeri.
question: Cuius generis hominum cognitionibus se numquam interfuisse Plinius minor Traiano scribens fatetur?
question_en: At the trials of what kind of people does Pliny the Younger, writing to Trajan, confess he had never been present?
derivation: The famous letter 10.96, in which Pliny consults Trajan on how to handle Christians, opens by admitting he had never attended cognitiones de Christianis. Entity-anchored (Pliny + Christians), short answer supported verbatim, closed-book famous.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Affirmabant autem hanc fuisse summam vel culpae suae vel erroris, quod essent soliti stato die ante lucem convenire, carmenque Christo quasi deo dicere secum invicem.
question: Cui Christiani, ut Plinio confessi sunt, stato die ante lucem coeuntes carmen quasi deo invicem dicere soliti erant?
question_en: To whom, as the Christians confessed to Pliny, were they accustomed to recite a hymn as to a god, gathering before dawn on a fixed day, in turn?
derivation: The celebrated description of early Christian worship: they met before dawn on a fixed day and sang 'carmen Christo quasi deo dicere secum invicem'. Entity-anchored (Christians, Christ), short name answer supported verbatim, closed-book famous.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Interrogavi ipsos an essent Christiani. Confitentes iterum ac tertio interrogavi supplicium minatus; perseverantes duci iussi.
question: Quid Plinius, supplicium minatus, de iis fieri iussit qui pertinaciter se Christianos esse confitebantur?
question_en: What did Pliny, having threatened punishment, order to be done to those who persistently confessed they were Christians?
answer_en: He ordered them led off (to execution).
derivation: Pliny's procedure: those who persisted in confessing (perseverantes) he ordered 'duci', i.e. led off to execution, holding that obstinacy must be punished. Entity-anchored (Pliny, Christians), short verbal answer supported verbatim.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Conquirendi non sunt; si deferantur et arguantur, puniendi sunt.
question: Quid Traianus, Plinio rescribens, de Christianis conquirendis statuit?
question_en: What did Trajan rule, in his reply to Pliny, about hunting out Christians?
answer_en: That they are not to be sought out.
derivation: Trajan's rescript (10.97), the first of its two famous rulings: Christians 'conquirendi non sunt' (they are not to be searched out, though they are to be punished if denounced and convicted). Entity-anchored (Trajan, Christians), short answer supported verbatim, closed-book famous.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Sine auctore vero propositi libelli in nullo crimine locum habere debent. Nam et pessimi exempli nec nostri saeculi est.
question: Quem locum Traianus libellis sine auctore propositis in criminibus tribuendum esse negavit?
answer: Nullum: in nullo crimine locum habere debent.
question_en: What standing did Trajan deny should be granted to anonymous written accusations in any charge?
answer_en: None: they are to have no place in any charge.
derivation: The second famous ruling of Trajan's rescript: anonymous denunciations ('sine auctore propositi libelli') are to have no place in any charge, being a bad precedent unworthy of the age. Entity-anchored (Trajan), short answer supported verbatim, closed-book famous.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Cautum est, domine, Pompeia lege quae Bithynis data est, ne quis capiat magistratum neve sit in senatu minor annorum triginta.
question: Minor quot annorum, ex lege Pompeia Bithynis data, magistratum capere aut in senatu esse non poterat?
question_en: Younger than how many years, by the lex Pompeia given to the Bithynians, could a man not hold a magistracy or sit in the senate?
derivation: Institutional fact: the lex Pompeia (Pompey's organization of Bithynia) barred anyone under thirty from holding local magistracy or sitting in the local senate. Entity-anchored (lex Pompeia, Bithynia), number answer supported verbatim ('minor annorum triginta').

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Tu, domine, dispice an instituendum putes collegium fabrorum dumtaxat hominum CL.
question: Quod collegium Plinius, post vastissimum Nicomediae incendium, instituendum Traiano proposuit?
question_en: What guild did Pliny propose to Trajan should be established after a devastating fire at Nicomedia?
answer_en: A guild of workmen (a fire brigade, collegium fabrorum).
derivation: After a fire devastated Nicomedia, Pliny proposed establishing a collegium fabrorum (capped at 150 men) to fight fires; Trajan refused (10.34), fearing such associations would quickly become political clubs (hetaeriae). Entity-anchored (Pliny, Nicomedia), short answer; a recognizable exchange in the history of Roman associations.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Tuo tamen desiderio subscripsi et dedisse me ius trium liberorum Suetonio Tranquillo ea condicione, qua assuevi, referri in commentarios meos iussi.
question: Cui viro erudito, postea 'De vita Caesarum' auctori, Plinius a Traiano ius trium liberorum impetravit?
question_en: For which learned man, later author of the 'Lives of the Caesars', did Pliny obtain from Trajan the 'right of three children'?
derivation: Pliny was the patron of the biographer Suetonius and secured the ius trium liberorum for him from Trajan. Entity-anchored to Suetonius; single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Suetonius's link to Pliny is well known; the descriptor 'author of De vita Caesarum' is a true external identifier.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: In aquae ductum, domine, Nicomedenses impenderunt HS XXX CCCXVIII, qui imperfectus adhuc omissus, destructus etiam est; rursus in alium ductum erogata sunt CC.
question: Quae civitas, ut Plinius Traiano scribit, magnam pecuniam in aquae ductus imperfectos frustra erogaverat?
question_en: Which city, as Pliny writes to Trajan, had wastefully spent a great sum of money on unfinished aqueducts?
derivation: Building-project fact: the Nicomedians twice spent large sums on aqueducts that were left unfinished and even pulled down; Pliny asks Trajan for an engineer to finish the work (10.37-38). Entity-anchored to Nicomedia, a major city of the province; short place answer supported by the source.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: C. Plinius Tacito suo s. Petis ut tibi avunculi mei exitum scribam, quo verius tradere posteris possis.
question: Quis a Plinio minore petivit ut avunculi sui exitum scriberet, quo verius posteris traderetur?
