question_en: Who asked Pliny the Younger to write an account of his uncle's death, so that it could be handed down to posterity more truly?
derivation: Addressee fact: the letter is to Tacitus ('C. Plinius Tacito suo s.'), who had requested the account ('Petis ut ... scribam, quo verius tradere posteris possis'). Closed-book: it is famously to the historian Tacitus that Pliny described the elder Pliny's death and the Vesuvius eruption. Entity-anchored, single-name answer.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Petis ut tibi avunculi mei exitum scribam, quo verius tradere posteris possis.
question: Quo gradu necessitudinis vir ille, cuius mortem Plinius minor ad Tacitum perscripsit, scriptori coniunctus erat?
question_en: By what degree of kinship was the man whose death Pliny the Younger described to Tacitus related to the writer?
answer_en: He was his maternal uncle (his mother's brother).
derivation: Relationship fact: the dead man is 'avunculus meus' (Pliny the Younger's maternal uncle), i.e. Pliny the Elder; avunculus = mother's brother (Plinia was the Elder's sister). Closed-book, well-known; entity-anchored to both Plinys and the eruption.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Erat Miseni classemque imperio praesens regebat.
question: Cui rei Plinius maior, cum Vesuvius erumperet, Miseni praeerat?
question_en: What was Pliny the Elder in command of at Misenum when Vesuvius erupted?
answer_en: The fleet (he was prefect of the fleet).
derivation: Command fact: 'Erat Miseni classemque imperio praesens regebat' — he was at Misenum commanding the fleet (praefectus classis Misenensis). Entity-anchored to Pliny the Elder and Misenum; short answer; closed-book.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Nubes — incertum procul intuentibus ex quo monte; Vesuvium fuisse postea cognitum est — oriebatur, cuius similitudinem et formam non alia magis arbor quam pinus expresserit.
question: Ex quo monte nubem illam ortam esse postea cognitum esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: From which mountain does Pliny report it was afterwards recognized that the cloud had risen?
derivation: The eruption mountain: 'Vesuvium fuisse postea cognitum est.' Closed-book famous; entity-anchored, single place answer; the canonical fact of the letter.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Nonum Kal. Septembres hora fere septima mater mea indicat ei apparere nubem inusitata et magnitudine et specie.
question: Quo die mater Plinii minoris fratri suo nubem inusitatam apparere indicavit?
question_en: On what day did Pliny the Younger's mother point out to her brother the appearance of an extraordinary cloud?
answer_en: On the ninth day before the Kalends of September (24 August).
derivation: Date fact: 'Nonum Kal. Septembres' = a.d. IX Kal. Sept. = 24 August (AD 79), the traditional date of the eruption. The 'mater mea' (Pliny the Younger's mother) was sister of Pliny the Elder, hence 'fratri suo.' Entity-anchored, date answer; closed-book famous.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Nubes — incertum procul intuentibus ex quo monte; Vesuvium fuisse postea cognitum est — oriebatur, cuius similitudinem et formam non alia magis arbor quam pinus expresserit. Nam longissimo velut trunco elata in altum quibusdam ramis diffundebatur.
question: Cui arbori potissimum similem fuisse nubem e Vesuvio ortam Plinius scribit?
question_en: To what tree above all does Pliny say the cloud that rose from Vesuvius was most similar?
derivation: Famous simile: the eruption column shaped 'non alia magis arbor quam pinus' — a long trunk spreading into branches at the top (umbrella pine). Translatable (a tree, not wordplay), entity-anchored, short answer; one of the best-known images in Latin literature.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Egrediebatur domo; accipit codicillos Rectinae Tasci imminenti periculo exterritae — nam villa eius subiacebat, nec ulla nisi navibus fuga -: ut se tanto discrimini eriperet orabat.
question: Cuius mulieris codicillos accepit Plinius maior, quae perterrita ut se periculo eriperet orabat?
question_en: Whose written note did Pliny the Elder receive, a woman who in terror begged to be rescued from the danger?
derivation: Named appeal: 'accipit codicillos Rectinae Tasci ... ut se tanto discrimini eriperet orabat.' Rectina's message turned his scientific reconnaissance into a rescue mission. Entity-anchored named person, single answer.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Cunctatus paulum an retro flecteret, mox gubernatori ut ita faceret monenti 'Fortes' inquit 'fortuna iuvat: Pomponianum pete.'
question: Quem virum petere Plinius maior gubernatorem iussit, cum diceret 'fortes fortuna iuvat'?
question_en: Whom did Pliny the Elder order the helmsman to make for, saying 'fortune favors the brave'?
derivation: Named destination: 'Pomponianum pete' — he sailed on to join Pomponianus (at Stabiae). Entity-anchored named person; short answer; the maxim 'fortes fortuna iuvat' anchors the moment.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: 'Fortes' inquit 'fortuna iuvat: Pomponianum pete.' Stabiis erat diremptus sinu medio — nam sensim circumactis curvatisque litoribus mare infunditur.
question: In quo oppido Pomponianus, ad quem Plinius maior navigavit ibique periit, morabatur?
question_en: In what town was Pomponianus staying, the man to whom Pliny the Elder sailed and where he died?
derivation: Place fact: 'Stabiis erat' (Pomponianus at Stabiae); the elder Pliny reached him there and the death narrative unfolds at Stabiae. Famous death place of Pliny the Elder; entity-anchored, single place answer.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Dubito, constantiam vocare an imprudentiam debeam — agebam enim duodevicensimum annum -: posco librum Titi Livi, et quasi per otium lego atque etiam ut coeperam excerpo.
question: Quotum aetatis annum agebat Plinius minor, cum Vesuvius erumperet?
question_en: Which year of his age was Pliny the Younger in when Vesuvius erupted?
derivation: Age fact: 'agebam enim duodevicensimum annum' — Pliny the Younger was in his eighteenth year at the eruption (AD 79). Entity-anchored, ordinal/number answer; closed-book.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: posco librum Titi Livi, et quasi per otium lego atque etiam ut coeperam excerpo.
question: Cuius scriptoris librum Plinius minor, Vesuvio iam erumpente, poposcit et legebat?
question_en: Whose book did Pliny the Younger call for and read while Vesuvius was already erupting?
derivation: Famous detail: 'posco librum Titi Livi ... lego atque ... excerpo.' Entity-anchored to Pliny the Younger and Livy; single-name answer; closed-book.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Hic situs est Rufus, pulso qui Vindice quondam imperium asseruit non sibi sed patriae.
question: Quem Verginius Rufus, ut in epitaphio quod sibi composuit apud Plinium legitur, pepulisse se gloriatur?
question_en: Whom does Verginius Rufus boast, in the epitaph he composed for himself and recorded by Pliny, to have driven out?
derivation: Historical fact: in letter 6.10 about Verginius Rufus's tomb, his self-composed epitaph reads 'pulso ... Vindice' — having suppressed the revolt of Vindex (AD 68) he claimed empire 'not for himself but for the fatherland.' Entity-anchored, single-name answer; closed-book famous.

author: Pliny the Younger
source_text: Accusavi Marium Priscum, qui lege repetundarum damnatus utebatur clementia legis, cuius severitatem immanitate criminum excesserat; relegatus est.
question: Quem virum Plinius lege repetundarum accusavit, qui damnatus relegatus est?
question_en: Whom did Pliny prosecute under the extortion law, a man who was condemned and relegated?
derivation: First-person fact: 'Accusavi Marium Priscum ... lege repetundarum damnatus ... relegatus est.' The celebrated extortion trial of Marius Priscus, proconsul of Africa. Entity-anchored to Pliny and Marius Priscus; single-name answer; closed-book.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: orbem certe dicimus terrae globumque verticibus includi fatemur.
question: Quam figuram terrae ipsius esse Plinius adfirmat?
question_en: What shape does Pliny affirm the earth itself to have?
answer_en: The shape of a globe (a sphere).
derivation: The roundness of the earth: Pliny says we call it the orb of the earth and admit it is a globe enclosed by poles, and elsewhere argues it from ships vanishing over the horizon (2.164) and the rounding of water. Entity-anchored to the earth; short answer (a sphere) supported verbatim by orbem... terrae globumque. Indirect statement governed by adfirmat. Closed-book: the sphericity of the earth is a textbook tenet of ancient cosmology.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Hanc ergo formam eius aeterno et inrequieto ambitu, inenarrabili celeritate, viginti quattuor horarum spatio circumagi solis exortus et occasus haut dubium reliquere.
question: Quot horarum spatio totum mundum semel circumagi Plinius tradit?
question_en: In how many hours does Pliny say the whole world turns around once?
answer_en: In the space of twenty-four hours.
derivation: Number fact: the heaven/world completes one rotation in 24 hours (sunrise to sunrise). Entity-anchored to the mundus; single numeric answer supported verbatim by viginti quattuor horarum spatio circumagi. Indirect statement (mundum circumagi) governed by tradit. Closed-book: the daily rotation of the celestial sphere is a commonplace of ancient (geocentric) astronomy.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: inter hanc caelumque eodem spiritu pendent certis discreta spatiis septem sidera, quae ab incessu vocamus errantia, cum errent nulla minus illis.
question: Quot sunt errantia sidera, quae inter terram et caelum pendere Plinius tradit?
question_en: How many wandering stars (planets) are there, which Pliny says hang between the earth and the sky?
derivation: The seven 'wandering stars' (the classical planetae, counting the sun and moon). Entity-anchored to the planets set between earth and heaven; single numeric answer (seven) supported verbatim by septem sidera... errantia. Closed-book: the seven planets are a fixture of ancient astronomy.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: eorum medius sol fertur, amplissima magnitudine ac potestate nec temporum modo terrarumque, sed siderum etiam ipsorum caelique rector.
question: Quod ex septem errantibus sideribus medium ferri et caeli rectorem esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: Which of the seven wandering stars does Pliny say moves in the middle and is the ruler of the heaven?
derivation: The sun's central place among the seven planets and its role as 'ruler.' Entity-anchored to the wandering stars; single named answer (the sun) supported verbatim by eorum medius sol fertur... caelique rector. Indirect statement governed by tradit. Closed-book.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: summum esse quod vocant Saturni sidus ideoque minimum videri et maximo ambire circulo ac tricesimo anno ad brevissima sedis suae principia regredi certum est.
question: Quod errans sidus et altissimum esse et tricesimo anno ad sedis suae principia redire Plinius tradit?
question_en: Which wandering star does Pliny say is both the highest and returns to the beginning of its course in the thirtieth year?
derivation: Saturn is the outermost/highest of the planets and has the longest period, returning in the thirtieth year. Entity-anchored to the wandering stars; single named answer (Saturn) supported verbatim by summum esse quod vocant Saturni sidus... tricesimo anno... regredi. Two acc.+inf. clauses (altissimum esse, redire) governed by tradit. Closed-book.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Sed omnium admirationem vincit novissimum sidus, terris familiarissimum et in tenebrarum remedium ab natura apertum, lunae.
question: Quod errantium siderum novissimum, id est terris proximum, esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: Which of the wandering stars does Pliny say is the lowest, that is, nearest to the earth?
derivation: The moon is the lowest (novissimum) of the seven planets and 'most familiar to the lands' (nearest), hence the smallest, fastest orbit (2.44). Entity-anchored to the wandering stars; single named answer (the moon) supported verbatim by novissimum sidus, terris familiarissimum... lunae. Closed-book: the moon as the nearest celestial body is basic ancient astronomy.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: solis fulgore, ut reliqua siderum, regi, siquidem in totum mutuata ab eo luce fulgere, qualem in repercussu aquae volitare conspicimus.
question: Unde lunam lumen suum habere Plinius tradit?
question_en: From where does Pliny say the moon has its light?
answer_en: From the sun, with borrowed light.
derivation: The moon shines not by its own light but with light wholly borrowed from the sun. Entity-anchored to the moon; short answer (from the sun) supported verbatim by solis fulgore... regi, siquidem in totum mutuata ab eo luce fulgere. Indirect statement governed by tradit. Closed-book: that the moon's light is reflected sunlight is a well-known ancient finding.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: quippe manifestum est solem interventu lunae occultari lunamque terrae obiectu ac vices reddi, eosdem solis radios luna interpositu suo auferente terrae terraque lunae.
question: Cuius rei interventu solem, cuius obiectu lunam deficere Plinius tradit?
answer: Solem interventu lunae, lunam obiectu terrae.
question_en: Through the interposition of what does Pliny say the sun is eclipsed, and through the obstruction of what the moon?
answer_en: The sun by the interposition of the moon, the moon by the obstruction (shadow) of the earth.
derivation: The mechanism of eclipses: a solar eclipse is the sun hidden by the moon coming between, a lunar eclipse is the moon falling into the earth's shadow/obstruction. Entity-anchored to the sun and moon; verifiable two-part answer supported verbatim by solem interventu lunae occultari lunamque terrae obiectu. Closed-book: the cause of eclipses is a canonical ancient fact.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: neque aliud esse noctem quam terrae umbram, figuram autem umbrae similem metae ac turbini inverso.
question: Quid esse noctem Plinius adfirmat?
question_en: What does Pliny affirm night to be?
answer_en: Nothing other than the shadow of the earth.
derivation: Night defined as nothing other than the earth's shadow (a consequence of the eclipse/shadow geometry). Entity-anchored to night and the earth; short answer supported verbatim by neque aliud esse noctem quam terrae umbram. Indirect statement governed by adfirmat. Closed-book and memorable.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: apud Graecos autem investigavit primus omnium Thales Milesius Olympiadis XLVIII anno quarto praedicto solis defectu, qui Alyatte rege factus est urbis conditae anno CLXX.
question: Quis Graecorum primus solis defectum praedixisse a Plinio traditur?
question_en: Which of the Greeks is recorded by Pliny as the first to have predicted a solar eclipse?
derivation: The famous prediction of a solar eclipse by Thales of Miletus (in the reign of Alyattes). Entity-anchored to the Greeks; single named answer supported verbatim by investigavit primus omnium Thales Milesius... praedicto solis defectu. Nominativus cum infinitivo (Thales praedixisse traditur). Closed-book and iconic in the history of science.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Infra solem ambit ingens sidus appellatum Veneris, alterno meatu vagum ipsisque cognominibus aemulum solis ac lunae. praeveniens quippe et ante matutinum exoriens luciferi nomen accepit ut sol alter diemque maturans, contra ab occasu refulgens nuncupatur vesper ut prorogans lucem vicemve lunae reddens.
question: Quibus nominibus stella Veneris appellatur cum ante matutinum exoritur et cum ab occasu refulget, secundum Plinium?
question_en: By what names is the star of Venus called when it rises before dawn and when it shines from the west (at sunset), according to Pliny?
answer_en: Lucifer (the morning star) and Vesper (the evening star).
derivation: The double name of the planet Venus: Lucifer as morning star, Vesper as evening star. Entity-anchored to Venus; verifiable two-name answer supported verbatim by luciferi nomen accepit... nuncupatur vesper. Closed-book: the morning/evening-star identity of Venus is a standard fact.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Veteres quattuor omnino servavere per totidem mundi partes—ideo nec Homerus plures nominat—hebeti, ut mox iudicatum est, ratione.
question: Quot ventos Homerus nominat, ut Plinius refert?
question_en: How many winds does Homer name, as Pliny reports?
derivation: The ancients reckoned only four winds, one for each quarter of the world, and Homer names no more than four. Entity-anchored to Homer; single numeric answer supported verbatim by Veteres quattuor omnino servavere... ideo nec Homerus plures nominat. Closed-book named-author fact.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: universum autem circuitum Eratosthenes, in omnium quidem litterarum subtilitate, sed in hac utique praeter ceteros solers, quem cunctis probari video, CCLII milium stadiorum prodidit.
question: Quot milium stadiorum universum terrae circuitum Eratosthenes prodidisse a Plinio traditur?
question_en: How many thousand stadia did Eratosthenes give for the whole circumference of the earth, according to Pliny?
derivation: Eratosthenes' celebrated measurement of the earth's circumference, 252,000 stadia. Entity-anchored to Eratosthenes; single numeric answer supported verbatim by Eratosthenes... CCLII milium stadiorum prodidit. Nominativus cum infinitivo (Eratosthenes prodidisse traditur). Closed-book and iconic in ancient geography/science.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Terrarum orbis universus in tres dividitur partes, Europam, Asiam, Africam.
question: In quot partes terrarum orbem universum dividi Plinius tradit, et quas?
answer: In tres partes: Europam, Asiam et Africam.
question_en: Into how many parts does Pliny say the whole world is divided, and which?
answer_en: Into three parts: Europe, Asia, and Africa.
derivation: Number-plus-names fact opening the geographical books. Anchored to the orbis terrarum; single verifiable answer (three named continents) supported verbatim. Indirect statement orbem dividi governed by tradit; closed-book because the tripartite division of the world is a commonplace of ancient geography.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: proximis autem faucibus utrimque inpositi montes coercent claustra, Abila Africae, Europae Calpe, laborum Herculis metae, quam ob causam indigenae columnas eius dei vocant.
question: Qui duo montes ad fauces oceani positi 'laborum Herculis metae' sive columnae Herculis a Plinio appellantur?
question_en: Which two mountains set on the strait of the ocean does Pliny call the 'limits of Hercules' labors,' i.e. the Pillars of Hercules?
derivation: Iconic Pillars of Hercules identification (Abila in Africa, Calpe in Europe). Two named entities, single checkable answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: among the best-known landmarks of ancient geography.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Hiberus amnis, navigabili commercio dives, ortus in Cantabris haut procul oppido Iuliobrica, per CCCCL p. fluens, navium per CCLX a Vareia oppido capax, quem propter universam Hispaniam Graeci appellavere Hiberiam.
question: A quo flumine Graeci universam Hispaniam Hiberiam appellaverunt secundum Plinium?
question_en: After which river did the Greeks name all of Spain 'Iberia,' according to Pliny?
derivation: Etymology of Iberia from the river Hiberus (Ebro). Entity-anchored (Spain, the Greeks, the river); single named answer supported verbatim by quem propter ... Graeci appellavere Hiberiam. Closed-book, recognizable geographic fact.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Pyrenaei montes Hispanias Galliasque disterminant promunturiis in duo diversa maria proiectis.
question: Qui montes Hispanias Galliasque inter se disterminant secundum Plinium?
question_en: Which mountains separate the Spains from the Gauls, according to Pliny?
derivation: Boundary fact: the Pyrenees divide Spain from Gaul. Two named regions, one mountain-range answer supported verbatim. Closed-book, textbook geography.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: praefari necessarium est auctorem nos Divum Augustum secuturos discriptionemque ab eo factam Italiae totius in regiones XI.
question: In quot regiones Divus Augustus Italiam totam discripsisse a Plinio traditur?
question_en: Into how many regions is the Deified Augustus said by Pliny to have divided all of Italy?
derivation: The famous Augustan division of Italy into eleven regiones, which structures the rest of the book. Anchored to Augustus + Italy; single number answer (XI) supported verbatim. Nominativus cum infinitivo (Augustus discripsisse traditur). Closed-book, attributed.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Est ergo folio maxime querno adsimulata, multo proceritate amplior quam latitudine.
question: Cui folio figuram Italiae maxime adsimilari Plinius scribit?
question_en: To which leaf does Pliny say the shape of Italy is most likened?
derivation: Pliny's well-known simile for the shape of Italy (an oak leaf). Subject (Italia) is the running topic; the question supplies it, making it decontextualizable. Short answer supported verbatim by folio querno adsimulata. Indirect statement governed by scribit.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: conplexa montes septem. ipsa dividitur in regiones XIIII, compita Larum CCLXV.
question: In quot regiones ipsa urbs Roma divisa est secundum Plinium?
question_en: Into how many regions is the city of Rome itself divided, according to Pliny?
derivation: The Augustan fourteen regiones of the city of Rome (distinct from the eleven regiones of Italy). Anchored to Rome; single number answer (XIV) supported verbatim. Question names urbs Roma so the source's ipsa is unambiguous. Closed-book.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Tiberis, ante Thyberis appellatus et prius Albula, e media fere longitudine Appennini finibus Arretinorum profluit.
question: Quo nomine Tiberis amnis antiquissime appellatus esse a Plinio dicitur?
question_en: By what name does Pliny say the river Tiber was called in earliest times?
derivation: The Tiber's oldest name. The text gives prius Albula (earlier than both Tiberis and Thyberis), so Albula is the earliest. Entity-anchored to the Tiber, single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: a recurring antiquarian fact in Latin literature.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: fluvius Rubico, quondam finis Italiae.
question: Qui fluvius quondam finis Italiae fuisse a Plinio dicitur?
question_en: Which river does Pliny say was once the boundary of Italy?
derivation: The Rubicon as the former boundary of Italy (proper). Single named-river answer supported verbatim by Rubico, quondam finis Italiae. Closed-book and iconic (Caesar's crossing).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Hirpinorum colonia una Beneventum auspicatius mutato nomine, quae quondam appellata Maleventum.
question: Quo nomine colonia Beneventum, ante nominis mutationem, quondam appellata est secundum Plinium?
question_en: By what name was the colony of Beneventum formerly called, before its name was changed, according to Pliny?
derivation: The renaming of Maleventum to the more auspicious Beneventum. Anchored to the town; single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book, frequently cited etymological/onomastic fact.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: oppidum Paestum, Graecis Posidonia appellatum, sinus Paestanus.
question: Quo nomine oppidum Paestum a Graecis appellatum esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: By what name do the Greeks call the town of Paestum, according to Pliny?
derivation: The Greek name of Paestum. Entity-anchored to the town; single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and recognizable (the Greek colony Poseidonia).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Padus, e gremio Vesuli montis celsissimum in cacumen Alpium elati finibus Ligurum Bagiennorum visendo fonte profluens condensque se cuniculo et in Forovibiensium agro iterum exoriens, nullo amnium claritate inferior, Graecis dictus Eridanus ac poena Phaethontis inlustratus.
question: Quo nomine Padus amnis a Graecis dictus esse a Plinio traditur?
question_en: By what name was the river Padus (Po) called by the Greeks, according to Pliny?
derivation: The Greek name of the Po, tied to the myth of Phaethon. Anchored to the Padus; single-name answer supported verbatim by Graecis dictus Eridanus. Closed-book, well-known.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Verum ante omnes claritate Sicilia, Sicania Thucydidi dicta, Trinacria pluribus aut Trinacia a triangula specie.
question: Quo nomine Sicilia a plerisque ob triangulam speciem appellata est secundum Plinium?
question_en: By what name is Sicily called by most people on account of its triangular shape, according to Pliny?
derivation: The name Trinacria for triangular Sicily. Anchored to Sicily; single-name answer supported verbatim by Trinacria ... a triangula specie. Closed-book, iconic (the island's three-cornered shape).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: in hoc tractu interierunt Boi, quorum tribus CXII fuisse auctor est Cato, item Senones, qui ceperunt Romam.
question: Quae Gallorum gens Romam cepisse a Plinio memoratur?
question_en: Which Gallic people does Pliny record as having captured Rome?
derivation: Attributes the sack of Rome to the Senones. Anchored to Rome + the Gauls; single named-people answer supported verbatim by Senones, qui ceperunt Romam. Closed-book (Brennus' Gauls, 390 BC).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: ex quibus Laevi et Marici condidere Ticinum non procul a Pado, sicut Boi Transalpibus profecti Laudem Pompeiam, Insubres Mediolanum.
question: Quae gens Mediolanum condidisse secundum Plinium traditur?
question_en: Which people is said by Pliny to have founded Mediolanum (Milan)?
derivation: Founder fact: the Insubres founded Mediolanum (the verb condidere governs the list, sicut ... Insubres Mediolanum). Anchored to the city; single named-people answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and recognizable (Milan).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Molossi, apud quos Dodonaei Iovis templum oraculo inlustre
question: Apud quam Epiri gentem templum Dodonaei Iovis, oraculo inlustre, situm esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: Among which people of Epirus does Pliny say the temple of Dodonaean Jupiter, famous for its oracle, is located?
derivation: The famous oracle and temple of Dodonaean Jupiter lies among the Molossi of Epirus. Anchored to Dodona plus Jupiter's oracle; single named-people answer supported verbatim by Molossi, apud quos Dodonaei Iovis templum oraculo inlustre. Closed-book: Dodona is among the most famous Greek oracles. Indirect statement templum situm esse governed by tradit.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: a quo VII p. introrsus liberum oppidum Delphi sub monte Parnaso, clarissimi in terris oraculi Apollinis.
question: Sub quo monte oppidum Delphi, cum clarissimo Apollinis oraculo, situm esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: Under which mountain does Pliny say the town of Delphi, with its most famous oracle of Apollo, is situated?
derivation: The location of Delphi, seat of the most famous oracle of Apollo, beneath Mount Parnassus. Anchored to Delphi plus Apollo's oracle; single named-mountain answer supported verbatim by Delphi sub monte Parnaso. Closed-book, iconic. Indirect statement oppidum situm esse governed by tradit.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Peloponnesus, Apia antea appellata et Pelasgia, paeninsula haut ulli terrae nobilitate postferenda, inter duo maria Aegeum et Ionium, platani folio similis propter angulosos recessus, circuitu DLXIII p. colligit auctore Isidoro.
question: Cui folio Peloponnesum propter angulosos recessus similem esse Plinius scribit?
question_en: To which leaf does Pliny say the Peloponnese is similar, on account of its angular indentations?
derivation: Pliny's well-known simile for the shape of the Peloponnese (a plane-tree leaf), paralleling the oak-leaf simile for Italy in Book III. Anchored to the Peloponnese; short answer (folio platani) supported verbatim by platani folio similis. Indirect statement Peloponnesum similem esse governed by scribit; closed-book, recognizable geographic image.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: intus delubrum Olympii Iovis, ludorum claritate fastos Graeciae complexum, Pisaeorum quondam oppidum, praefluente Alpheo amne.
question: Quo amne praefluente delubrum Olympii Iovis, ludorum claritate nobile, situm esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: By which river flowing past does Pliny say the temple of Olympian Jupiter, famous for its games, stands?
derivation: Olympia, site of the temple of Olympian Jupiter and the Olympic games, lies by the river Alpheus. Anchored to Olympian Jupiter plus the games; single named-river answer supported verbatim by praefluente Alpheo amne. Closed-book, iconic (the Alpheus of Olympia). Ablative absolute in question; indirect statement delubrum situm esse governed by tradit.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: et ante cunctos claritate Penius, ortos iuxta Gomphos interque Ossam et Olympum nemorosa convalle defluens D stadiis, dimidio eius spatii navigabilis.
question: Inter quos montes Penium amnem nemorosa convalle defluere Plinius tradit?
question_en: Between which two mountains does Pliny say the river Peneus flows through a wooded valley?
derivation: The river Peneus runs through a wooded valley (the Vale of Tempe) between Mounts Ossa and Olympus in Thessaly. Anchored to the Peneus; two named mountains as answer, supported verbatim by interque Ossam et Olympum nemorosa convalle defluens. Closed-book, iconic (Tempe; the two great mountains of Thessaly). Indirect statement Penium defluere governed by tradit.

author: Pliny the Elder

source_text: Per haec ac talia maxima aetatis parte transacta quinquagesimo anno imperium cepit quantumuis mirabili casu.
question: Quoto aetatis anno Claudius imperium cepit, ut Suetonius tradit?
question_en: In which year of his age did Claudius take power, according to Suetonius?
derivation: Age-at-accession fact, supported by 'quinquagesimo anno imperium cepit.' Ordinal answer, entity-anchored to Claudius, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Verum postero die et senatu segniore in exeqvendis conatibus per taedium ac dissensionem diversa censentium et multitudine, quae circumstabat, unum rectorem iam et nominatim exposcente, armatos pro contione iurare in nomen suum passus est promisitque singulis quina dena sestertia, primus Caesarum fidem militis etiam praemio pigneratus.
question: Quantum praemium Claudius singulis militibus promisit, primus Caesarum fidem militis praemio pigneratus?
question_en: What bounty did Claudius promise to each soldier, being the first of the Caesars to secure the soldiers' loyalty even with a reward?
derivation: The accession donative to the praetorians who made him emperor; supported by 'promisitque singulis quina dena sestertia, primus Caesarum fidem militis etiam praemio pigneratus.' Number fact, entity-anchored to Claudius; closed-book (the famous first imperial accession donative).

author: Suetonius
source_text: Cum decretis sibi a senatu ornamentis triumphalibus leviorem maiestati principali titulum arbitraretur velletque iusti triumphi decus, unde adquireret Britanniam potissimum elegit, neque temptatam ulli post Diuum Iulium et tunc tumultuantem ob non redditos transfugas.
question: Quam insulam Claudius, post Diuum Iulium a nullo temptatam, expeditione sua in deditionem recepit?
question_en: Which island, untried by anyone since the deified Julius, did Claudius receive in surrender by his expedition?
derivation: Claudius's annexation of Britain, his sole military expedition, supported by 'unde adquireret Britanniam potissimum elegit, neque temptatam ulli post Diuum Iulium.' Place answer, anchored to Claudius and Julius Caesar; iconic closed-book fact.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Fucinum adgressus est non minus conpendii spe quam gloriae, cum quidam privato sumptu emissuros se repromitterent, si sibi siccati agri concederentur. Per tria autem passuum milia partim effosso monte partim exciso canalem absoluit aegre et post undecim annos, quamuis continuis XXX hominum milibus sine intermissione operantibus.
question: Quot hominum milia Claudius in emissario Fucini lacus per undecim annos perficiendo adhibuit?
question_en: How many thousands of men did Claudius employ over eleven years to complete the outlet of the Fucine Lake?
derivation: The draining of Lake Fucinus, supported by 'post undecim annos, quamuis continuis XXX hominum milibus ... operantibus.' Number fact, entity-anchored to the Fucine project; closed-book engineering work.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Iudaeos impulsore Chresto assidue tumultuantis Roma expulit.
question: Quam gentem Claudius, impulsore Chresto assidue tumultuantem, Roma expulit?
question_en: Which people, continually rioting at the instigation of Chrestus, did Claudius expel from Rome?
derivation: The expulsion of the Jews from Rome (cf. Acts 18:2), supported verbatim. Entity-anchored (Claudius + 'impulsore Chresto'), single-noun answer, closed-book famous.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Verum inlecebris Agrippinae, Germanici fratris sui filiae, per ius osculi et blanditiarum occasiones pellectus in amorem, subornavit proximo senatu qui censerent, cogendum se ad ducendum eam uxorem, quasi rei p. maxime interesset, dandamque ceteris veniam talium coniugiorum, quae ad id tempus incesta habebantur.
question: Quam feminam, Germanici fratris sui filiam, Claudius novissimam uxorem duxit?
question_en: Which woman, the daughter of his brother Germanicus, did Claudius take as his last wife?
derivation: Claudius married his niece Agrippina the Younger (daughter of his brother Germanicus, and Nero's mother), supported by 'inlecebris Agrippinae, Germanici fratris sui filiae ... cogendum se ad ducendum eam uxorem.' Entity-anchored, surfaces the brother-relation, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Liberos ex tribus uxoribus tulit: ex Vrgulanilla Drusum et Claudiam, ex Paetina Antoniam, ex Messalina Octaviam et quem primo Germanicum, mox Britannicum cognominavit.
question: Quos liberos Claudius ex uxore Messalina suscepit?
question_en: Which children did Claudius have by his wife Messalina?
derivation: Supported by 'ex Messalina Octaviam et quem primo Germanicum, mox Britannicum cognominavit.' Names both children; entity-anchored to Claudius and Messalina; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Antoniam Cn. Pompeio Magno, deinde Fausto Sullae, nobilissimis iuvenibus, Octaviam Neroni priuigno suo collocavit, Silano ante desponsam.
question: Cui Claudius filiam Octaviam in matrimonium collocavit?
question_en: To whom did Claudius give his daughter Octavia in marriage?
derivation: Supported by 'Octaviam Neroni priuigno suo collocavit.' Nero was his stepson, adopted son, and successor. Entity-anchored, single-name answer, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: novas etiam commentus est litteras tres ac numero veterum quasi maxime necessarias addidit; de quarum ratione cum privatus adhuc volumen edidisset, mox princeps non difficulter optinuit ut in usu quoque promiscuo essent.
question: Quot novas litteras Claudius excogitavit et veterum numero addidit?
question_en: How many new letters did Claudius devise and add to the existing alphabet?
derivation: Claudius's three new letters added to the Latin alphabet, supported by 'novas etiam commentus est litteras tres ... addidit.' Number fact, entity-anchored, closed-book famous.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Historiam in adulescentia hortante T. Livio, Sulpicio vero Flauo etiam adiuuante, scribere adgressus est.
question: Quo auctore hortante Claudius adulescens historiam scribere adgressus est?
question_en: At whose urging did the young Claudius undertake to write history?
derivation: Supported by 'Historiam in adulescentia hortante T. Livio ... scribere adgressus est.' Entity-anchored to Claudius and Livy, single-name answer, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Et veneno quidem occisum convenit; ubi autem et per quem dato, discrepat. Quidam tradunt epulanti in arce cum sacerdotibus per Halotum spadonem praegustatorem; alii domestico convivio per ipsam Agrippinam, quae boletum medicatum auidissimo ciborum talium optulerat.
question: Quo cibo medicato Claudius, ut plerique tradunt, veneno necatus est?
question_en: By which poisoned food, as most report, was Claudius killed?
derivation: The canonical account of Claudius's death by a poisoned mushroom offered by Agrippina, supported by 'veneno quidem occisum convenit ... per ipsam Agrippinam, quae boletum medicatum ... optulerat.' Entity-anchored, short answer, closed-book famous.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Excessit III. Id. Octob. Asinio Marcello Acilio Auiola coss. sexagesimo quarto aetatis, imperii quarto decimo anno, funeratusque est sollemni principum pompa et in numerum deorum relatus; quem honorem a Nerone destitutum abolitumque recepit mox per Vespasianum.
question: Quoto aetatis anno Claudius decessit, ut Suetonius tradit?
question_en: In which year of his age did Claudius die, according to Suetonius?
derivation: Age-at-death fact, supported by 'sexagesimo quarto aetatis.' Ordinal answer, entity-anchored, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Excessit III. Id. Octob. Asinio Marcello Acilio Auiola coss. sexagesimo quarto aetatis, imperii quarto decimo anno, funeratusque est sollemni principum pompa et in numerum deorum relatus; quem honorem a Nerone destitutum abolitumque recepit mox per Vespasianum.
question: Quoto imperii anno Claudius decessit, ut Suetonius tradit?
question_en: In which year of his reign did Claudius die, according to Suetonius?
derivation: Reign-length fact (AD 41-54), supported by 'imperii quarto decimo anno.' Ordinal answer, entity-anchored, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Excessit III. Id. Octob. Asinio Marcello Acilio Auiola coss. sexagesimo quarto aetatis, imperii quarto decimo anno, funeratusque est sollemni principum pompa et in numerum deorum relatus; quem honorem a Nerone destitutum abolitumque recepit mox per Vespasianum.
question: Per quem principem Claudius honorem divinum a Nerone abolitum recepit?
question_en: Through which emperor did Claudius regain the divine honor that Nero had abolished?
derivation: Claudius was deified at death; Nero let the honor lapse and Vespasian restored it, supported by 'in numerum deorum relatus; quem honorem a Nerone destitutum abolitumque recepit mox per Vespasianum.' Entity-anchored (Claudius, Nero, Vespasian), single-name answer, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Domitianus natus est VIIII. Kal. Novemb. patre consule designato inituroque mense insequenti honorem, regione urbis sexta ad Malum Punicum, domo quam postea in templum gentis Flaviae convertit.
question: Quo die natum esse Domitianum Suetonius tradit?
answer: Ante diem nonum Kalendas Novembres (VIIII Kal. Novemb.).
question_en: On what day does Suetonius say Domitian was born?
answer_en: On the ninth day before the Kalends of November (24 October).
derivation: Birth-date fact, anchored to Domitian. Supported verbatim by 'Domitianus natus est VIIII. Kal. Novemb.' Indirect statement (natum esse) under tradit. Closed-book: the birth-date (24 October AD 51) of a major emperor; short calendrical answer.

author: Suetonius
source_text: regione urbis sexta ad Malum Punicum, domo quam postea in templum gentis Flaviae convertit.
question: In quod templum Domitianus domum, in qua natus erat, postea convertit?
question_en: Into what temple did Domitian later convert the house in which he had been born?
answer_en: Into the temple of the Flavian gens.
derivation: Building/family fact: Domitian's birth-house (in Rome's sixth region) was later turned into the Templum Gentis Flaviae, the dynastic shrine of the Flavians. Supported verbatim by 'domo quam postea in templum gentis Flaviae convertit.' Entity-anchored to Domitian; single named-monument answer.

author: Suetonius
source_text: contrectatis multorum uxoribus, Domitiam Longinam Aelio Lamiae nuptam etiam in matrimonium abduxit, atque uno die super XX. officia urbana aut peregrina distribuit.
question: Quam feminam, Aelio Lamiae nuptam, Domitianus in matrimonium abduxit?
question_en: Which woman, married to Aelius Lamia, did Domitian carry off into marriage?
derivation: Family fact: Domitian's wife was Domitia Longina, whom he took from her husband Aelius Lamia. Supported verbatim by 'Domitiam Longinam Aelio Lamiae nuptam etiam in matrimonium abduxit.' Entity-anchored to Domitian + Aelius Lamia; single-name answer; closed-book (Domitia Longina, daughter of Corbulo, is the well-known empress).

author: Suetonius
source_text: habitabat cum patre una, sellamque eius ac fratris, quotiens prodirent, lectica sequebatur ac triumphum utriusque Iudaicum equo albo comitatus est.
question: Quo equo Domitianus triumphum Iudaicum patris fratrisque comitatus est?
question_en: On what horse did Domitian accompany the Jewish triumph of his father and brother?
derivation: Career detail: Domitian rode a white horse in the Jewish triumph of his father Vespasian and brother Titus (AD 71). Supported verbatim by 'triumphum utriusque Iudaicum equo albo comitatus est.' Entity-anchored to Domitian + the Jewish triumph; short, concrete answer.

author: Suetonius
source_text: nec quicquam amplius quam muscas captare ac stilo praeacuto configere; ut cuidam interroganti, essetne quis intus cum Caesare, non absurde responsum sit a Vibio Crispo, ne muscam quidem.
question: Quid Vibius Crispus respondit interroganti num quis intus cum Domitiano esset?
question_en: What did Vibius Crispus reply to the man who asked whether anyone was inside with Domitian?
derivation: Famous joke: Domitian spent his hours stabbing flies, so when asked if anyone was with Caesar, Vibius Crispus quipped 'not even a fly.' Supported verbatim. Entity-anchored to Vibius Crispus + Domitian; the witticism survives translation; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Instituit et quinquennale certamen Capitolino Iovi triplex, musicum, equestre, gymnicum, et aliquanto plurium quam nunc est coronatorum.
question: In cuius dei honorem Domitianus quinquennale certamen triplex instituit?
question_en: In whose honor did Domitian establish a triple quinquennial contest?
derivation: Institutional fact: Domitian founded the quinquennial Capitoline Games (musical, equestrian, gymnastic) in honor of Capitoline Jupiter. Supported verbatim by 'quinquennale certamen Capitolino Iovi triplex.' Entity-anchored to Domitian + Capitoline Jupiter; single-name answer; the Agon Capitolinus is a recognized institution.

author: Suetonius
source_text: De Chattis Dacisque post varia proelia duplicem triumphum egit.
question: De quibus gentibus Domitianus duplicem triumphum egit?
question_en: Over which peoples did Domitian celebrate a double triumph?
answer_en: Over the Chatti and the Dacians.
derivation: Military fact: a double triumph over the Chatti and the Dacians. Supported verbatim by 'De Chattis Dacisque ... duplicem triumphum egit.' Entity-anchored to Domitian + named peoples; short list answer.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Bellum civile motum a L. Antonio, superioris Germaniae praeside, confecit absens felicitate mira.
question: Quis, superioris Germaniae praeses, bellum civile adversus Domitianum movit?
question_en: Who, as governor of Upper Germany, stirred up civil war against Domitian?
derivation: Historical fact: the revolt of L. Antonius Saturninus, governor of Upper Germany (AD 89), put down in Domitian's absence. Supported verbatim by 'Bellum civile motum a L. Antonio, superioris Germaniae praeside.' Entity-anchored to Domitian + the office; single-name answer (cognomen Saturninus supplied only in the gloss, not the text).

author: Suetonius
source_text: Iunium Rusticum, quod Paeti Thraseae et Helvidii Prisci laudes edidisset appellassetque eos sanctissimos viros; cuius criminis occasione philosophos omnis urbe Italiaque summovit.
question: Quos Domitianus, occasione damnati Iunii Rustici, urbe Italiaque summovit?
question_en: Whom did Domitian expel from Rome and Italy, on the occasion of the condemnation of Junius Rusticus?
derivation: Historical fact: Domitian's expulsion of philosophers from Rome and Italy, occasioned by the condemnation of Junius Rusticus (who had praised Thrasea Paetus and Helvidius Priscus). Supported verbatim by 'philosophos omnis urbe Italiaque summovit.' Entity-anchored to Domitian + Junius Rusticus; short answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Pari arrogantia, cum procuratorum suorum nomine formalem dictaret epistulam, sic coepit: "Dominus et deus noster hoc fieri iubet." Vnde institutum posthac, ut ne scripto quidem ac sermone cuiusquam appellaretur aliter.
question: Quibus verbis se appellari Domitianus voluit, cum epistulam procuratorum suorum nomine dictaret?
question_en: By what words did Domitian want himself to be addressed, when he dictated a letter in the name of his procurators?
derivation: Iconic fact: Domitian had himself styled 'dominus et deus,' beginning an official letter 'Our lord and god orders this,' and thereafter was addressed no otherwise. Supported verbatim. Entity-anchored to Domitian; the title survives translation; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Consulatus septemdecim cepit, quot ante eum nemo; ex quibus septem medios continuavit, omnes autem paene titulo tenus gessit.
question: Quot consulatus Domitianus cepit, quot ante eum nemo gesserat?
question_en: How many consulships did Domitian hold, more than anyone before him?
derivation: Number fact: Domitian held seventeen consulships, more than any predecessor. Supported verbatim by 'Consulatus septemdecim cepit, quot ante eum nemo.' Entity-anchored to Domitian; single-number answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Post autem duos triumphos Germanici cognomine assumpto Septembrem mensem et Octobrem ex appellationibus suis Germanico Domitianumque transnominavit, quod altero suscepisset imperium, altero natus esset.
question: In quae nomina Domitianus menses Septembrem et Octobrem transnominavit?
answer: Septembrem in Germanicum, Octobrem in Domitianum.
question_en: Into what names did Domitian rename the months of September and October?
derivation: Naming fact: Domitian renamed September 'Germanicus' (the month he had taken up the empire) and October 'Domitianus' (the month he was born). Supported verbatim by 'Septembrem mensem et Octobrem ... Germanico Domitianumque transnominavit.' Entity-anchored to Domitian; short paired answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Per haec terribilis cunctis et invisus, tandem oppressus est amicorum libertorumque intimorum conspiratione, simul et uxoris.
question: Qua coniuratione Domitianus tandem oppressus est?
answer: Amicorum libertorumque intimorum, simul et uxoris.
question_en: By what conspiracy was Domitian at last overthrown?
answer_en: By a conspiracy of his intimate friends and freedmen, together with his wife.
derivation: Death fact: Domitian was killed by a palace conspiracy of his closest friends and freedmen, joined by his wife. Supported verbatim by 'oppressus est amicorum libertorumque intimorum conspiratione, simul et uxoris.' Entity-anchored to Domitian; short phrase answer; closed-book (the assassination of AD 96).

author: Suetonius
source_text: Stephanus, Domitillae procurator, et tunc interceptarum pecuniarum reus, consilium operamque optulit. Ac sinisteriore brachio, velut aegro, lanis fasciisque per aliquot dies ad avertendam suspicionem obvoluto, ad ipsam horam dolorem interiecit; professusque conspirationis indicium et ob hos admissus, legenti traditum a se libellum et attonito suffodit inguina.
question: Quis Domitiano, legenti libellum, primum vulnus intulit, inguina suffodiens?
question_en: Who struck the first blow at Domitian, stabbing him in the groin while he read a document?
derivation: Assassination fact: the steward Stephanus struck the first blow, stabbing Domitian in the groin as he read a handed-over document. Supported verbatim by 'Stephanus, Domitillae procurator ... legenti traditum a se libellum et attonito suffodit inguina.' Entity-anchored; single-name answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Occisus est XIIII. Kal. Octob. anno aetatis quadragensimo quinto, imperii quinto decimo.
question: Quotum aetatis annum agens Domitianus occisus est?
question_en: In which year of his age was Domitian killed?
derivation: Age-at-death fact. Supported verbatim by 'anno aetatis quadragensimo quinto.' Ordinal/number answer, entity-anchored to Domitian; closed-book (killed AD 96, aged 44/45). Source retains the Latin Library spelling 'quadragensimo' for 'quadragesimo.'

author: Suetonius
source_text: Occisus est XIIII. Kal. Octob. anno aetatis quadragensimo quinto, imperii quinto decimo.
question: Quoto imperii anno Domitianus occisus est?
question_en: In which year of his reign was Domitian killed?
derivation: Reign-length fact: Domitian was killed in the fifteenth year of his reign (AD 81-96). Supported verbatim by 'imperii quinto decimo.' Ordinal/number answer, entity-anchored to Domitian; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Contra senatus adeo laetatus est, ut repleta certatim curia non temperaret, quin mortuum contumeliosissimo atque acerbissimo adclamationum genere laceraret, scalas etiam inferri clipeosque et imagines eius coram detrahi et ibidem solo affligi iuberet, novissime eradendos ubique titulos abolendamque omnes memoriam decerneret.
question: Quid senatus de Domitiano occiso decrevit, titulos eius ubique eradi iubens?
question_en: What did the senate decree about the slain Domitian, ordering his inscriptions to be erased everywhere?
answer_en: That all memory of him be abolished (the damnatio memoriae).
derivation: Historical fact: the senate rejoiced at Domitian's death and decreed his inscriptions erased and all memory of him abolished (damnatio memoriae). Supported verbatim by 'novissime eradendos ubique titulos abolendamque omnes memoriam decerneret.' Entity-anchored to the senate + Domitian; short noun-phrase answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Corneliam Cinnae quater consulis filiam duxit uxorem, ex qua illi mox Iulia nata est; neque ut repudiaret compelli a dictatore Sulla ullo modo potuit.
question: Cuius filiam Corneliam Caesar primam uxorem duxit?
question_en: Whose daughter Cornelia did Caesar take as his first wife?
derivation: First-wife fact: Cornelia, daughter of Cinna (consul four times); Caesar refused even Sulla's demand to divorce her. Anchored to Caesar + Cornelia + Cinna; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book, iconic.

author: Suetonius
source_text: circa Pharmacussam insulam a praedonibus captus est mansitque apud eos non sine summa indignatione prope quadraginta dies cum uno medico et cubicularis duobus. nam comites seruosque ceteros initio statim ad expediendas pecunias, quibus redimeretur, dimiserat. numeratis deinde quinquaginta talentis expositus in litore non distulit quin e uestigio classe deducta persequeretur abeuntis ac redactos in potestatem supplicio, quod saepe illis minatus inter iocum fuerat, adficeret.
question: Quot talentis Caesar a praedonibus, qui eum circa Pharmacussam insulam ceperant, se redemit?
question_en: For how many talents did Caesar ransom himself from the pirates who had captured him near the island of Pharmacussa?
derivation: Ransom number, anchored to Caesar + pirates + Pharmacussa. Single verifiable number (quinquaginta talentis) in source; the famous pirate-capture episode. Closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: et in amitae quidem laudatione de eius ac patris sui utraque origine sic refert: 'Amitae meae Iuliae maternum genus ab regibus ortum, paternum cum diis inmortalibus coniunctum est. nam ab Anco Marcio sunt Marcii Reges, quo nomine fuit mater; a Venere Iulii, cuius gentis familia est nostra.'
question: A qua dea gentem Iuliam ortam esse Caesar in laudatione amitae suae Iuliae adfirmavit?
question_en: From which goddess did Caesar declare the gens Iulia descended, in the eulogy of his aunt Iulia?
derivation: From Caesar's funeral oration for his aunt Iulia (covers the aunt-Iulia ask). Indirect statement (gentem...ortam esse) under adfirmavit. Anchored to gens Iulia + Venus; single named answer, supported verbatim. Iconic (Venus Genetrix).

author: Suetonius
source_text: Deposita prouinciae spe pontificatum maximum petit non sine profusissima largitione; in qua reputans magnitudinem aeris alieni, cum mane ad comitia descenderet, praedixisse matri osculanti fertur domum se nisi pontificem non reuersurum. atque ita potentissimos duos competitores multumque et aetate et dignitate antecedentes superauit, ut plura ipse in eorum tribubus suffragia quam uterque in omnibus tulerit.
question: Quod sacerdotium amplissimum Caesar, duobus potentioribus competitoribus superatis, adeptus est?
question_en: Which supreme priesthood did Caesar obtain, defeating two more powerful competitors?
derivation: Office fact, anchored to Caesar; he won the pontificatus maximus over two older, more distinguished rivals. Single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Igitur cum Bibulo consul creatur.
question: Quo collega Caesar primum consulatum gessit?
question_en: With which colleague did Caesar hold his first consulship?
derivation: Colleague fact: Caesar's first consulship was shared with Bibulus (praenomen Marcus given earlier in the same chapter, 'Marcoque Bibulo'). Anchored to Caesar + consulship; iconic ('Iulius and Caesar' joke that follows). Single named answer.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Sub idem tempus Calpurniam L. Pisonis filiam successuri sibi in consulatu duxit uxorem suamque, Iuliam, Gnaeo Pompeio conlocauit repudiato priore sponso Seruilio Caepione, cuius uel praecipua opera paulo ante Bibulum inpugnauerat.
question: Cuius filiam Calpurniam Caesar uxorem duxit?
question_en: Whose daughter Calpurnia did Caesar take as wife?
derivation: Marriage fact: Calpurnia, daughter of L. Piso (consul-designate to succeed Caesar). Anchored to Caesar + Calpurnia + Piso; single named answer supported verbatim.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Sub idem tempus Calpurniam L. Pisonis filiam successuri sibi in consulatu duxit uxorem suamque, Iuliam, Gnaeo Pompeio conlocauit repudiato priore sponso Seruilio Caepione, cuius uel praecipua opera paulo ante Bibulum inpugnauerat.
question: Cui Caesar filiam suam Iuliam in matrimonium collocavit?
question_en: To whom did Caesar give his daughter Iulia in marriage?
derivation: Relation fact: Caesar married his daughter Iulia to Pompey (sealing the alliance). Anchored to Caesar + Iulia + Pompey; single named answer supported verbatim. Iconic.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Germanos, qui trans Rhenum incolunt, primus Romanorum ponte fabricato adgressus maximis adfecit cladibus; adgressus est et Britannos ignotos antea superatisque pecunias et obsides imperauit.
question: Quis primus Romanorum, ut Suetonius tradit, Germanos trans Rhenum incolentes ponte fabricato adgressus est?
question_en: Who was the first Roman, according to Suetonius, to attack the Germans living across the Rhine by building a bridge?
derivation: 'primus Romanorum' fact, anchored to Germans + Rhine + bridge; the famous Rhine-bridge campaigns. Single answer (Caesar) decontextualized by the named entities. Closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: consecutusque cohortis ad Rubiconem flumen, qui prouinciae eius finis erat, paulum constitit, ac reputans quantum moliretur, conuersus ad proximos: 'etiam nunc,' inquit, 'regredi possumus; quod si ponticulum transierimus, omnia armis agenda erunt.'
question: Quod flumen prouinciae Caesaris finis erat, quo transito ille bellum ciuile incohavit?
question_en: Which river was the boundary of Caesar's province, by crossing which he began the civil war?

author: Suetonius

question_en: Which grandsons did Tiberius leave as equal heirs in his will?
answer_en: Gaius, son of Germanicus, and Tiberius, son of Drusus.
derivation: Tiberius's will named two grandsons as equal heirs; supported verbatim. Gaius (Caligula) became his successor, Tiberius being Gemellus. Entity-anchored, accusative answer, closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Titus cognomine paterno, amor ac deliciae generis humani, (tantum illi ad promerendam omnium voluntatem vel ingenii vel artis vel fortunae superfuit, et, quod difficillimum est, in imperio: quando privatus atque etiam sub patre principe ne odio quidem, nedum vituperatione publica caruit), natus est III. Kal. Ian.
question: Quo praeconio Suetonius Titum imperatorem in vitae principio appellat?
question_en: By what acclamation does Suetonius hail the emperor Titus at the start of his life?
answer_en: The love and darling of the human race.
derivation: The famous Suetonian judgment on Titus. Supported verbatim by the appositive 'amor ac deliciae generis humani.' Entity-anchored to Titus; closed-book, as this is among the most quoted epithets of any emperor. Answer cast in accusative as the predicate of appellat.

author: Suetonius
source_text: educatus in aula cum Britannico simul, ac paribus disciplinis et apud eosdem magistros institutus.
question: Cum quo Titus in aula educatus est, paribus disciplinis et apud eosdem magistros institutus?
question_en: With whom was Titus brought up in the palace, schooled in the same studies under the same teachers?
answer_en: With Britannicus (son of the emperor Claudius).
derivation: Biographical fact: Titus was reared alongside Britannicus, Claudius's son. Supported verbatim by 'educatus in aula cum Britannico simul.' Entity-anchored to Titus + Britannicus; single-name answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: eodemque tempore Arrecinam Tertullam, patre eq. R. sed praefecto quodam praetorianarum cohortium, duxit uxorem et in defunctae locum Marciam Furnillam splendidi generis; cum qua, sublata filia, divortium fecit.
question: Quas uxores Titus duxit, primum unam, deinde in defunctae locum alteram?
question_en: Which wives did Titus marry, one first and then a second in place of the deceased?
derivation: Family fact: the two wives of Titus. Supported verbatim by 'Arrecinam Tertullam ... duxit uxorem et in defunctae locum Marciam Furnillam.' Entity-anchored to Titus; bounded two-name answer (cf. the multi-name set answers in the Vespasian file).

author: Suetonius
source_text: Ex questurae deinde honore legioni praepositus, Taricheas et Gamalam urbes Iudaeae validissimas in potestate redegit.
question: Quas urbes Iudaeae validissimas Titus, legioni praepositus, in potestatem redegit?
question_en: Which very strong cities of Judaea did Titus, put in command of a legion, bring under his power?
derivation: Career fact from the Jewish war. Supported verbatim by 'Taricheas et Gamalam urbes Iudaeae validissimas in potestate redegit.' Entity-anchored to Titus + Judaea; two named-place answer. (source_text keeps the Latin Library reading 'in potestate redegit' for 'in potestatem redegit.')

author: Suetonius
source_text: Cuius brevi compos, et ad perdomandam Iudaeam relictus, novissima Hierosolymorum oppugnatione duodecim propugnatores totidem sagittarum confecit ictibus, cepitque ea natali filiae suae tanto militum gaudio ac favore, ut in gratulatione imperatorem eum consalutaverint.
question: Quam urbem Titus, ad perdomandam Iudaeam relictus, novissima oppugnatione cepit?
question_en: Which city did Titus, left to subdue Judaea, capture in the final assault?
derivation: The famous conquest: Titus took Jerusalem in the final assault of the Jewish war (AD 70). Supported by 'novissima Hierosolymorum oppugnatione ... cepitque ea.' Entity-anchored to Titus + Jerusalem; single-place answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Triumphavit cum patre censuramque gessit una, eidem collega et in tribunicia potestate et in septem consulatibus fuit.
question: In quot consulatibus Titus patri Vespasiano collega fuit?
question_en: In how many consulships was Titus a colleague to his father Vespasian?
derivation: Number/office fact: Titus shared seven consulships with his father. Supported verbatim by 'in septem consulatibus fuit.' Entity-anchored to Titus + Vespasian; single-number answer.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Berenicen statim ab urbe dimisit, invitus, invitam.
question: Quam reginam Titus, princeps factus, statim ab urbe dimisit, invitus invitam?
question_en: Which queen did Titus, on becoming emperor, immediately send away from Rome, unwilling though she too was unwilling?
derivation: Famous episode: Titus dismissed Queen Berenice from Rome on his accession. Supported verbatim by 'Berenicen statim ab urbe dimisit, invitus, invitam.' Entity-anchored to Titus + Berenice; single-name answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Et tamen nemine ante se munificentia minor, amphitheatro dedicato thermisque iuxta celeriter exstructis, munus edidit apparatissimum largissimusque; dedit et navale proelium in veteri naumachia, ibidem et gladiatores atque uno die quinque milia omne genus ferarum.
question: Quod opus Titus dedicavit, thermis iuxta celeriter exstructis, cum munus apparatissimum ederet?
question_en: What structure did Titus dedicate, with baths quickly built nearby, when he gave a most lavish show?
answer_en: The amphitheatre (the Flavian Amphitheatre, the Colosseum).
derivation: Building fact: Titus dedicated the amphitheatre (the Colosseum) and built adjacent baths. Supported verbatim by 'amphitheatro dedicato thermisque iuxta celeriter exstructis.' Entity-anchored to Titus; single-answer; the most famous act of his reign.

author: Suetonius
source_text: atque etiam recordatus quondam super cenam, quod nihil cuiquam toto die praestitisset, memorabilem illam meritoque laudatam vocem edidit: "Amici, diem perdidi."
question: Quam memorabilem vocem Titus edidit, cum recordatus esset se nihil cuiquam toto die praestitisse?
question_en: What memorable saying did Titus utter when he recalled that he had done no one a kindness the whole day?
answer_en: Friends, I have lost a day.
derivation: The most famous saying of Titus. Supported verbatim by the quoted 'Amici, diem perdidi.' Entity-anchored to Titus; survives translation; closed-book. Indirect statement (se ... praestitisse) under recordatus esset.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Quaedam sub eo fortuita ac tristia acciderunt, ut conflagratio Vesevi montis in Campania, et incendium Romae per triduum totidemque noctes, item pestilentia quanta non temere alias.
question: Cuius montis conflagratio in Campania sub Tito principe accidit?
question_en: The eruption of which mountain occurred in Campania during the reign of Titus?
derivation: The eruption of Vesuvius (AD 79), the great disaster of Titus's reign. Supported verbatim by 'conflagratio Vesevi montis in Campania.' Entity-anchored to Titus's reign + Campania; single-place answer; closed-book. (source_text keeps the Latin Library spelling 'Vesevi' for 'Vesuvii'.)

author: Suetonius
source_text: Pontificatum maximum ideo se professus accipere ut puras servaret manus, fidem praestitit.
question: Quod sacerdotium Titus se accipere professus est, ut puras servaret manus?
question_en: Which priesthood did Titus profess to take up in order to keep his hands clean?
answer_en: The office of pontifex maximus (chief priesthood).
derivation: Office fact: Titus said he accepted the pontificate maximus to keep his hands pure. Supported verbatim by 'Pontificatum maximum ideo se professus accipere ut puras servaret manus.' Entity-anchored to Titus; single-office answer; indirect statement (se accipere) under professus.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Fratrem insidiari sibi non desinentem, sed paene ex professo sollicitantem exercitus, meditantem fugam, neque occidere neque seponere ac ne in minore quidem honore habere sustinuit, sed, ut a primo imperii die, consorte successoremque testari perseveravit.
question: Quem Titus, quamvis sibi insidiantem, a primo imperii die consortem ac successorem imperii testari perseveravit?
question_en: Whom did Titus, although he kept plotting against him, persist in declaring his partner and successor in the empire from the first day of his reign?
derivation: Succession fact: Titus persisted in naming his brother (Domitian, who did succeed him) as partner and heir despite his plotting. Supported by 'Fratrem ... consorte successoremque testari perseveravit'; the brother of Titus is Domitian. Entity-anchored to Titus + Domitian; closed-book. (source_text keeps the Latin Library reading 'consorte' for 'consortem'.)

author: Suetonius
source_text: Excessit in eadem qua pater villa Id. Septb. post biennium ac menses duos diesque XX. quam successerat patri, altero et quadragesimo aetatis anno.
question: Cui Titus in principatu successit?
question_en: Whom did Titus succeed as emperor?
derivation: Succession fact: Titus succeeded his father. Supported verbatim by 'quam successerat patri'; the father of Titus is Vespasian. Entity-anchored to Titus; single-name answer; closed-book (the Flavian succession).

author: Suetonius
source_text: Excessit in eadem qua pater villa Id. Septb. post biennium ac menses duos diesque XX. quam successerat patri, altero et quadragesimo aetatis anno.
question: In qua villa Titus mortuus est?
question_en: In what villa did Titus die?
answer_en: In the same villa as his father (the Sabine villa at Aquae Cutiliae).
derivation: Death-place fact: Titus died in the same villa as his father Vespasian (Aquae Cutiliae in the Sabine country; cf. 'Sabinos petiit' in ch. 10). Supported verbatim by 'Excessit in eadem qua pater villa.' Entity-anchored to Titus; place answer; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Excessit in eadem qua pater villa Id. Septb. post biennium ac menses duos diesque XX. quam successerat patri, altero et quadragesimo aetatis anno.
question: Quamdiu Titus, postquam patri successit, imperium tenuit?
answer: Biennium ac menses duos diesque viginti.
question_en: How long did Titus hold power after he had succeeded his father?
answer_en: Two years, two months, and twenty days.
derivation: Reign-length fact. Supported verbatim by 'post biennium ac menses duos diesque XX. quam successerat patri.' Entity-anchored to Titus; precise duration answer (accusative of extent); closed-book (his famously short reign).

author: Suetonius
source_text: Excessit in eadem qua pater villa Id. Septb. post biennium ac menses duos diesque XX. quam successerat patri, altero et quadragesimo aetatis anno.
question: Quotum aetatis annum agens Titus decessit?
question_en: In which year of his age did Titus die?
derivation: Age-at-death fact. Supported verbatim by 'altero et quadragesimo aetatis anno.' Ordinal/number answer, entity-anchored to Titus; closed-book (he died in AD 81, in his early forties).

author: Suetonius
source_text: Rebellione trium principum et caede incertum diu et quasi vagum imperium suscepit firmavitque tandem gens Flavia, obscura illa quidem ac sine ullis maiorum imaginibus, sed tamen rei p. nequaquam paenitenda.
question: Quae gens, ut Suetonius scribit, imperium diu incertum ac vagum tandem suscepit firmavitque?
question_en: Which family, as Suetonius writes, finally took up and made firm the empire that had long been uncertain and adrift?
derivation: The founding of the Flavian dynasty (Vespasian, then his sons Titus and Domitian). Anchored to the gens Flavia; single-entity answer supported verbatim by 'suscepit firmavitque tandem gens Flavia.' Closed-book: the rise of the Flavians after the year of the four emperors.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Vespasianus natus est in Sabinis ultra Reate vico modico, cui nomen est Phalacrinae, XV. kal. Dec. vesperi, Q. Sulpicio Camerino C. Poppaeo Sabino cons., quinquennio ante quam Augustus excederet.
question: Quo in loco, in Sabinis ultra Reate, Vespasianum natum esse Suetonius tradit?
answer: In vico cui nomen Phalacrinae, ultra Reate.
question_en: In what place, in the Sabine country beyond Reate, does Suetonius say Vespasian was born?
answer_en: In the village called Phalacrinae, beyond Reate.
derivation: Birthplace fact, anchored to Vespasian. Supported verbatim by 'in Sabinis ultra Reate vico modico, cui nomen est Phalacrinae.' Indirect statement (natum esse) under tradit. Closed-book: Vespasian's Sabine birthplace near Reate is a standard biographical fact.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Postea faenus apud Helvetios exercuit ibique diem obiit superstitibus uxore Vespasia Polla et duobus ex ea liberis, quorum maior Sabinus ad praefecturam urbis, minor Vespasianus ad principatum usque processit.
question: Quo nomine appellata est mater Vespasiani imperatoris?
question_en: By what name was the mother of the emperor Vespasian called?
derivation: Family fact. The source names Vespasia Polla as the wife (of Vespasian's father) and mother of the two sons, of whom the younger, Vespasian, reached the principate. Entity-anchored to Vespasian; single-name answer supported verbatim.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Inter haec Flaviam Domitillam duxit uxorem, Statilii Capellae equitis R. Sabratensis ex Africa delicatam olim Latinaeque condicionis, sed mox ingenuam et civem Rom. reciperatorio iudicio pronuntiatam.
question: Quam Vespasianus uxorem duxit, ex qua liberos suscepit?
question_en: Whom did Vespasian take as his wife, from whom he had his children?
derivation: Family fact. Supported verbatim by 'Flaviam Domitillam duxit uxorem.' Entity-anchored to Vespasian; single-name answer. Closed-book: his wife, mother of Titus and Domitian.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Ex hac liberos tulit Titum et Domitianum et Domitillam.
question: Quos liberos Vespasianus ex Flavia Domitilla tulit?
question_en: What children did Vespasian have by Flavia Domitilla?
derivation: Family fact. Supported verbatim by 'Ex hac liberos tulit Titum et Domitianum et Domitillam.' Entity-anchored to Vespasian and Flavia Domitilla; the two sons, Titus and Domitian, each later became emperor. Short list answer.

author: Suetonius
source_text: inde in Britanniam translatus tricies cum hoste conflixit. Duas validissimas gentes superque viginti oppida et insulam Vectem Britanniae proximan in dicionem redegit, partim Auli Plautii legati consularis, partim Claudi ipsius ductu.
question: Quam insulam Britanniae proximam Vespasianus, in Britannia rem gerens, in dicionem redegit?
question_en: Which island next to Britain did Vespasian, while campaigning in Britain, bring under his control?
answer_en: The island of Vectis (the Isle of Wight).
derivation: Career fact: under Claudius, Vespasian campaigned in Britain and subdued the island of Vectis (Isle of Wight). Supported verbatim by 'insulam Vectem Britanniae proximan in dicionem redegit.' Entity-anchored to Vespasian + Britain + the named island; single place answer. (source_text retains the Latin Library OCR slip 'proximan' for 'proximam'.)

author: Suetonius
source_text: Additis igitur ad copias duabus legionibus, octo alis, cohortibus decem, atque inter legatos maiore filio assumpto, ut primum provinciam attigit, proximas quoque convertit in se.
question: Quem filium suum Vespasianus, dux in bello Iudaico, inter legatos sibi assumpsit?
question_en: Which of his sons did Vespasian, as commander in the Jewish war, take to himself among his legates?
derivation: Career fact: in the Jewish war (under Nero) Vespasian took his elder son Titus among his legates. Supported by 'inter legatos maiore filio assumpto'; the elder son is Titus (named ch. 3). Entity-anchored to Vespasian + Titus + the Jewish war; short answer.

author: Suetonius
source_text: et unus ex nobilibus captivis Iosephus, cum coiceretur in vincula, constantissime asseveravit fore ut ab eodem brevi solveretur, verum iam imperatore.
question: Quis ex nobilibus captivis, in vincula coniectus, Vespasianum brevi imperatorem fore praedixit?
question_en: Which of the noble captives, when thrown into chains, predicted that Vespasian would soon be emperor?
derivation: Famous anecdote: the captured Jewish leader Josephus declared that Vespasian would soon free him, but as emperor. Supported by 'unus ex nobilibus captivis Iosephus ... asseveravit fore ut ab eodem brevi solveretur, verum iam imperatore.' Entity-anchored to Josephus + Vespasian; single-name answer; closed-book (a well-known episode of Josephus's life).

author: Suetonius
source_text: Ceterum divulgato facto, Tiberius Alexander praefectus Aegypti primus in verba Vespasiani legiones adegit Kal. Iul., qui principatus dies in posterum observatus est.
question: Quis praefectus Aegypti primus legiones in verba Vespasiani adegit?
question_en: Which prefect of Egypt was the first to swear his legions into allegiance to Vespasian?
derivation: Accession fact (AD 69). Supported verbatim by 'Tiberius Alexander praefectus Aegypti primus in verba Vespasiani legiones adegit Kal. Iul.'; that day (1 July) was thereafter kept as Vespasian's dies imperii. Entity-anchored, single-name answer; the proclamation of Vespasian while in the East.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Talis tantaque cum fama in urbem reversus, acto de Iudaeis triumpho, consulatus octo veteri addidit; suscepit et censuram.
question: De qua gente Vespasianus, in urbem reversus, triumphum egit?
question_en: Over what people did Vespasian, on returning to the city, celebrate a triumph?
derivation: Career fact: the Jewish triumph (AD 71). Supported verbatim by 'acto de Iudaeis triumpho.' Entity-anchored to Vespasian + the Jews; short answer. Closed-book: the famous triumph over Judaea, commemorated on the Arch of Titus.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Fecit et nova opera templum Pacis foro proximum, Divique Claudii in Caelio monte coeptum quidem ab Agrippina, sed a Nerone prope funditus destructum; item amphitheatrum urbe media, ut destinasse compererat Augustum.
question: Quod novum opus Vespasianus urbe media exstruere coepit, quod Augustum destinasse compererat?
question_en: What new structure did Vespasian begin to build in the middle of the city, which he had learned Augustus had planned?
answer_en: An amphitheatre (the Flavian Amphitheatre, the Colosseum).
derivation: Building fact: the Flavian Amphitheatre (Colosseum), begun by Vespasian in the city center. Supported verbatim by 'item amphitheatrum urbe media.' Entity-anchored to Vespasian; single answer; the most famous Flavian monument.

author: Suetonius
source_text: Reprehendenti filio Tito, quod etiam urinae vectigal commentus esset, pecuniam ex prima pensione admovit ad nares, sciscitans num odore offenderetur; et illo negante: Atqui, inquit, e lotio est.
question: Quid Vespasianus filio Tito respondit, cum is urinae vectigal a patre excogitatum reprehenderet?
question_en: What did Vespasian reply to his son Titus, when Titus criticized the tax on urine devised by his father?
answer_en: And yet it comes from urine.
derivation: The iconic 'pecunia non olet' episode: Titus objected to the urine tax, and Vespasian held a coin to his nose, saying 'Atqui, e lotio est' ('And yet it's from urine'). Supported verbatim. Entity-anchored to Vespasian + Titus + the urine tax; the saying survives translation and is among the most famous in Suetonius.

author: Suetonius
source_text: prima quoque morbi accessione: Vae, inquit, puto, deus fio.
question: Quid Vespasianus per iocum dixit, cum primum morbo, quo postea periit, corriperetur?
question_en: What did Vespasian jokingly say when he was first seized by the illness of which he later died?
answer_en: Woe, I think I am becoming a god.
derivation: Vespasian's dying jest at the onset of his final illness, mocking the deification of emperors. Supported verbatim by 'prima quoque morbi accessione: Vae, inquit, puto, deus fio.' Entity-anchored to Vespasian; the famous saying survives translation; closed-book.

author: Suetonius
source_text: alvo repente usque ad defectionem soluta, imperatorem, ait statem mori oportere; dumque consurgit ac mititur, inter manus sublevantium extinctus est VIIII. Kal. Iul.
question: Quid Vespasianus moriens dixit imperatorem facere oportere?
question_en: What did the dying Vespasian say an emperor ought to do?
answer_en: Die standing (an emperor ought to die on his feet).
derivation: Vespasian's last famous saying, that an emperor ought to die standing; he died in the act of rising, held up by his attendants. Entity-anchored to Vespasian; translatable; closed-book. (source_text retains the Latin Library OCR slips 'statem' for 'stantem' and 'mititur' for 'nititur'.)

author: Suetonius
source_text: Consulatu suo nono temptatus in Campania motiunculis levibus protinusque urbe repetita, Cutilias ac Reatina rura, ubi aestivare quotannis solebat, petit.
question: Quo Vespasianus, valetudine temptatus, ex urbe se contulit, ubi mox decessit?
question_en: To what place did Vespasian, when his health failed, withdraw from the city, where he soon died?
answer_en: To Cutiliae and the Reatine country (near Reate).
derivation: Death-place fact: Vespasian fell ill and died at Cutiliae (Aquae Cutiliae) in the Reatine country near Reate, his usual summer retreat. Supported verbatim by 'Cutilias ac Reatina rura ... petit'; he died there (ch. 24, 'inter manus sublevantium extinctus est'). Entity-anchored; place answer.

author: Suetonius
source_text: inter manus sublevantium extinctus est VIIII. Kal. Iul. annum agens aetatis sexagensimum ac nonum, superque mensem ac diem septimum.
question: Quotum aetatis annum agens Vespasianus decessit, ut Suetonius tradit?
question_en: In which year of his age did Vespasian die, according to Suetonius?
derivation: Age-at-death fact. Supported verbatim by 'annum agens aetatis sexagensimum ac nonum.' Ordinal/number answer, entity-anchored to Vespasian; closed-book (he died in AD 79, aged 69). (source_text retains the Latin Library spelling 'sexagensimum' for 'sexagesimum'.)

author: Suetonius
source_text: Convenit inter omnis, tam certum eum de sua suorumque genitura semper fuisse, ut post assiduas in se coniurationes ausus sit adfirmare senatui, ut filios sibi successuros aut neminem.
question: Quos Vespasianus senatui adfirmavit sibi successuros esse aut neminem?
question_en: Whom did Vespasian declare to the senate would succeed him, or else no one would?
derivation: Succession fact: Vespasian assured the senate that his sons would succeed him or no one. Supported verbatim by 'filios sibi successuros aut neminem'; his sons Titus, then Domitian, did in fact succeed him. Entity-anchored to Vespasian; short answer.

author: Suetonius (Vita Vergilii)
source_text: Natus est Gn. Pompeio Magno M. Licinio Crasso primum conss. Iduum Octobrium die in pago qui Andes dicitur et abest a Mantua non procul.
question: Quibus consulibus Vergilius natus est?
answer: Gn. Pompeio Magno et M. Licinio Crasso.
question_en: In whose consulship was Vergil born?
answer_en: When Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus and Marcus Licinius Crassus were consuls.
derivation: Birth-year fact (70 BC), anchored to Vergil and the named consular pair, supported verbatim by 'Gn. Pompeio Magno M. Licinio Crasso primum conss.' Closed-book: one of the canonical dates of Latin literary biography.

author: Suetonius (Vita Vergilii)
source_text: Natus est Gn. Pompeio Magno M. Licinio Crasso primum conss. Iduum Octobrium die in pago qui Andes dicitur et abest a Mantua non procul.
question: In quo pago prope Mantuam Vergilius natus esse traditur?
question_en: In what village near Mantua is Vergil said to have been born?
