source_text: Ad ea Antonius Primus (is acerrimus belli concitator) festinationem ipsis utilem, Vitellio exitiosam disseruit.
question: Quis dux partium Flavianarum, quem Tacitus acerrimum belli concitatorem appellat, festinationem belli adversus Vitellium suasit?
question_en: Which leader of the Flavian party, whom Tacitus calls the keenest instigator of the war, argued for haste in the war against Vitellius?
derivation: Anchored to the Flavian party + the man who pressed for speed; single named person, supported verbatim by 'Antonius Primus (is acerrimus belli concitator) festinationem ipsis utilem, Vitellio exitiosam disseruit'. Closed-book: Antonius Primus, the Flavian general who drove the Danubian legions into Italy in AD 69, is a stock figure of the year of the four emperors. The Tacitean tag 'acerrimus belli concitator' is reused as the anchor.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Quaesitum inde quae sedes bello legeretur. Verona potior visa, patentibus circum campis ad pugnam equestrem, qua praevalebant: simul coloniam copiis validam auferre Vitellio in rem famamque videbatur.
question: Quam urbem duces Flaviani sedem bello legerunt, propter campos circum patentis equestri pugnae aptos, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which city did the Flavian leaders choose as the seat of the war, on account of the open plains around it suited to cavalry battle, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to the Flavian leaders + their choice of base; single named place, supported verbatim by 'Verona potior visa, patentibus circum campis ad pugnam equestrem'. Mirrors the source's 'sedes bello legeretur'. Closed-book: Verona as the Flavian rallying-point before the advance on Cremona is a fixed point of the AD 69 campaign.

author: Tacitus
source_text: per quadriduum Cremona suffecit. cum omnia sacra profanaque in igne considerent, solum Mefitis templum stetit ante moenia, loco seu numine defensum.
question: Quod unum templum, ceteris omnibus Cremonae igne consumptis, ante moenia incolume stetit, ut Tacitus refert?
question_en: Which single temple, when all the rest of Cremona was consumed by fire, stood unharmed before the walls, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Cremona's burning + the one surviving temple; single named cult site, supported verbatim by 'solum Mefitis templum stetit ante moenia'. Closed-book: that only the temple of Mefitis survived the sack of Cremona is a memorable Tacitean detail. 'quod templum... stetit' indicative direct question.

author: Tacitus
source_text: per quadriduum Cremona suffecit. cum omnia sacra profanaque in igne considerent, solum Mefitis templum stetit ante moenia, loco seu numine defensum.
question: Per quot dies, capta urbe, direptio atque incendium Cremonae duravit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: For how many days did the sack of Cremona last, after the city was taken, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Cremona + the duration of its sack; single number, supported verbatim by 'per quadriduum Cremona suffecit' (Cremona held out / sufficed for the plundering four days). 'per quot dies' mirrors the durative 'per quadriduum'. Closed-book: the four-day sack and burning of Cremona by the victorious Flavian army is a notorious atrocity of AD 69.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Hic exitus Cremonae anno ducentesimo octogesimo sexto a primordio sui.
question: Quoto anno a primordio suo urbs Cremona, a Flavianis direpta atque incensa, deleta est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: In which year from its founding was the city of Cremona, sacked and burned by the Flavians, destroyed, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Cremona + its destruction; single ordinal number, supported verbatim by 'Hic exitus Cremonae anno ducentesimo octogesimo sexto a primordio sui'. Closed-book: Tacitus's dating of Cremona's fall to its 286th year is a stock fact marking the colony's age. 'quoto anno' mirrors the ordinal idiom.

author: Tacitus
source_text: sedem Iovis Optimi Maximi auspicato a maioribus pignus imperii conditam, quam non Porsenna dedita urbe neque Galli capta temerare potuissent, furore principum excindi.
question: Cuius dei aedes in Capitolio, dum Vitelliani et Flaviani Romae armis contendunt, incensa est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: The temple of which god on the Capitol was burned while the Vitellians and Flavians fought in arms at Rome, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to the Capitol + the deity whose temple burned; single named god, supported verbatim by 'sedem Iovis Optimi Maximi... furore principum excindi' (confirmed at 3.71 'sic Capitolium... conflagravit' and 3.72 'ea tunc aedes cremabatur'). Closed-book: the burning of the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus during the Flavian assault on Rome in AD 69 is one of the most famous calamities of the civil wars.

author: Tacitus
source_text: voverat Tarquinius Priscus rex bello Sabino, ieceratque fundamenta spe magis futurae magnitudinis quam quo modicae adhuc populi Romani res sufficerent.
question: Quis rex Romanus aedem Iovis Optimi Maximi bello Sabino vovit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which Roman king vowed the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus during the Sabine war, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to the temple of Jupiter O.M. + the king who vowed it; single named person, supported verbatim by 'voverat Tarquinius Priscus rex bello Sabino, ieceratque fundamenta' (antecedent: 'sedem Iovis Optimi Maximi' earlier in 3.72). Closed-book: that Tarquinius Priscus vowed and laid the foundations of the Capitoline temple of Jupiter is a stock fact of Roman tradition. 'vovit' + accusative.

author: Tacitus
source_text: At primores civitatis Flavium Sabinum praefectum urbis secretis sermonibus incitabant, victoriae famaeque partem capesseret.
question: Quod munus Romae Flavius Sabinus, Vespasiani frater, eo tempore gerebat, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which office at Rome did Flavius Sabinus, Vespasian's brother, hold at that time, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Flavius Sabinus + brother of Vespasian + his office; single named magistracy, supported verbatim by 'Flavium Sabinum praefectum urbis'. Closed-book: Flavius Sabinus, the elder brother of Vespasian and prefect of the city, killed in the Flavian struggle for Rome in AD 69, is a fixed figure of the year. 'praefecturam urbis' answers 'quod munus gerebat'.

author: Tacitus
source_text: innocentiam iustitiamque eius non argueres; sermonis nimius erat: id unum septem annis quibus Moesiam, duodecim quibus praefecturam urbis obtinuit, calumniatus est rumor.
question: Per quot annos Flavius Sabinus praefecturam urbis obtinuit, ut Tacitus refert?
question_en: For how many years did Flavius Sabinus hold the prefecture of the city, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Flavius Sabinus + the duration of his city prefecture; single number, supported verbatim by 'duodecim quibus praefecturam urbis obtinuit' (subject Sabinus, 'Hic exitus viri', 3.75). Closed-book number fact about Vespasian's brother's long tenure as praefectus urbi.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Domitianus prima inruptione apud aedituum occultatus, sollertia liberti lineo amictu turbae sacricolarum immixtus ignoratusque, apud Cornelium Primum paternum clientem iuxta Velabrum delituit.
question: Quis filius Vespasiani, capta a Vitellianis Capitolii arce, lineo amictu inter sacricolas occultatus evasit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which son of Vespasian escaped, hidden in a linen garment among the temple-worshippers, when the citadel of the Capitol was taken by the Vitellians, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to the son of Vespasian + his escape from the Capitol; single named person, supported verbatim by 'Domitianus... lineo amictu turbae sacricolarum immixtus ignoratusque... delituit'. Closed-book: Domitian's escape in disguise from the burning Capitol, before becoming emperor, is a famous episode of AD 69.

author: Tacitus
source_text: fessusque misero errore et pudenda latebra semet occultans ab Iulio Placido tribuno cohortis protrahitur.
question: Quis tribunus cohortis Vitellium in Palatio latentem protraxit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which cohort tribune dragged Vitellius out as he hid in the Palace, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Vitellius + the man who hauled him from hiding; single named person, supported verbatim by 'ab Iulio Placido tribuno cohortis protrahitur' (subject Vitellius, from 'in Palatium regreditur' earlier in 3.84). Closed-book: Vitellius's discovery in a wretched hiding place at the fall of Rome is a stock scene of his end.

author: Tacitus
source_text: postremo ad Gemonias, ubi corpus Flavii Sabini iacuerat, propulere. una vox non degeneris animi excepta, cum tribuno insultanti se tamen imperatorem eius fuisse respondit; ac deinde ingestis vulneribus concidit.
question: Quo loco Vitellium milites propulerunt, ubi antea Flavii Sabini corpus iacuerat, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: To what place did the soldiers drive Vitellius, where the body of Flavius Sabinus had earlier lain, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Vitellius + the place of his death + the prior fate of Sabinus's body; single named place, supported verbatim by 'postremo ad Gemonias, ubi corpus Flavii Sabini iacuerat, propulere'. Closed-book: Vitellius killed and his body cast on the Gemoniae, where Sabinus's body had lain, is the famous end of his reign.

author: Tacitus
source_text: septimum et quinquagensimum aetatis annum explebat, consulatum, sacerdotia, nomen locumque inter primores nulla sua industria, sed cuncta patris claritudine adeptus.
question: Quotum aetatis annum Vitellius, cum periit, explebat, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which year of his life was Vitellius completing when he died, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Vitellius + his age at death; single ordinal number, supported verbatim by 'septimum et quinquagensimum aetatis annum explebat' (subject Vitellius, just killed in 3.85). 'quotum aetatis annum... explebat' mirrors the source idiom. Closed-book biographical number, parallel to the recorded ages of the other emperors of AD 69.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Isdem diebus Fabius Valens Vrbini in custodia interficitur. caput eius Vitellianis cohortibus ostentatum ne quam ultra spem foverent.
question: In qua urbe Fabius Valens, dux Vitellianus, in custodia interfectus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: In which town was Fabius Valens, the Vitellian general, killed while in custody, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Fabius Valens + the Vitellian command + the place of his death; single named place, supported verbatim by 'Fabius Valens Vrbini in custodia interficitur' (Vrbini = locative of Urbinum). Closed-book: the capture and execution of the Vitellian general Fabius Valens at Urbinum, his severed head shown to his troops, is a key turning point before Rome's fall.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Cartimandua Brigantibus imperitabat, pollens nobilitate; et auxerat potentiam, postquam capto per dolum rege Carataco instruxisse triumphum Claudii Caesaris videbatur.
question: Cui genti Britanniae Cartimandua regina imperabat, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which people of Britain did Queen Cartimandua rule, per Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to Queen Cartimandua + the people she ruled; single named people, supported verbatim by 'Cartimandua Brigantibus imperitabat, pollens nobilitate'. 'imperabat' + dative mirrors 'imperitabat'. Closed-book: Cartimandua, queen of the Brigantes who handed over Caratacus, is a stock figure of Roman Britain.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Eiusdem anni principio Caesar Titus, perdomandae Iudaeae delectus a patre et privatis utriusque rebus militia clarus, maiore tum vi famaque agebat, certantibus provinciarum et exercituum studiis.
question: Quis perdomandae Iudaeae a patre delectus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Who was chosen by his father to subdue Judaea, according to Tacitus?
derivation: Opening fact of Book 5: Titus was put in charge of the Jewish war and the siege of Jerusalem. Anchored to Judaea + 'a patre'; single named answer, supported verbatim by 'Caesar Titus, perdomandae Iudaeae delectus a patre'. Closed-book: Titus's capture of Jerusalem (AD 70) is among the best-known facts of Roman history. The father is Vespasian.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Plurimi auctores consentiunt orta per Aegyptum tabe quae corpora foedaret, regem Bocchorim adito Hammonis oraculo remedium petentem purgare regnum et id genus hominum ut invisum deis alias in terras avehere iussum. Sic conquisitum collectumque vulgus, postquam vastis locis relictum sit, ceteris per lacrimas torpentibus, Moysen unum exulum monuisse ne quam deorum hominumve opem expectarent utrisque deserti, sed sibimet duce caelesti crederent, primo cuius auxilio praesentis miserias pepulissent.
question: Quo duce Iudaei ex Aegypto expulsi novas terras petiverunt, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Under whose leadership did the Jews, after being expelled from Egypt, seek new lands, according to Tacitus?
derivation: In the account Tacitus says most authorities agree on ('plurimi auctores consentiunt', 5.3), a plague in Egypt led king Bocchoris to drive out the Jews, and Moses, one of the exiles, became their leader. Anchored to the Jews + Egypt; single named leader, supported by 'Moysen unum exulum ... sibimet duce caelesti crederent'. Closed-book: Moses leading the Jews out of Egypt is among the most widely known facts across cultures. The rival origin theories (Cretan, Ethiopian, Assyrian, etc.) are dropped as multi-attributed and non-verifiable.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Septimo die otium placuisse ferunt, quia is finem laborum tulerit; dein blandiente inertia septimum quoque annum ignaviae datum.
question: Quoto quoque die Iudaeos otium agere Tacitus tradit?
question_en: On every which day does Tacitus report that the Jews keep rest?
derivation: The Sabbath. Anchored to the Jews + Tacitus; single ordinal-number answer, supported verbatim by 'Septimo die otium placuisse'. Indirect statement (Iudaeos otium agere) governed by tradit. Closed-book: the Jewish seventh-day rest is a stock fact; Tacitus's reported reason ('quia is finem laborum tulerit') is not asked, only the day.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Septimo die otium placuisse ferunt, quia is finem laborum tulerit; dein blandiente inertia septimum quoque annum ignaviae datum.
question: Quotum quemque annum Iudaeos ignaviae dare Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Every which year does Tacitus report the Jews give over to idleness?
derivation: The sabbatical year. Anchored to the Jews + Tacitus; single ordinal answer, supported verbatim by 'septimum quoque annum ignaviae datum'. Indirect statement (Iudaeos dare) governed by tradit. Closed-book ethnographic fact reported by Tacitus, distinct from the seventh-day rest.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Sue abstinent memoria cladis, quod ipsos scabies quondam turpaverat, cui id animal obnoxium.
question: Quo animali Iudaeos abstinere Tacitus tradit?
question_en: From which animal does Tacitus report that the Jews abstain?
derivation: Jewish abstention from pork. Anchored to the Jews + Tacitus; single named animal in the ablative (abstinere + abl.), supported verbatim by 'Sue abstinent'. Closed-book: abstaining from pork is a defining, widely known Jewish custom.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Aegyptii pleraque animalia effigiesque compositas venerantur, Iudaei mente sola unumque numen intellegunt: profanos qui deum imagines mortalibus materiis in species hominum effingant; summum illud et aeternum neque imitabile neque interiturum.
question: Quot numina Iudaeos mente sola intellegere Tacitus tradit?
question_en: How many deities does Tacitus report the Jews conceive with the mind alone?
derivation: Jewish monotheism. Anchored to the Jews (contrasted with the Egyptians) + Tacitus; single-number answer, supported verbatim by 'Iudaei mente sola unumque numen intellegunt'. Indirect statement (Iudaeos intellegere) governed by tradit. Closed-book: that the Jews worship one God is a stock fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Igitur nulla simulacra urbibus suis, nedum templis sistunt; non regibus haec adulatio, non Caesaribus honor.
question: Quot simulacra Iudaei in urbibus suis, nedum templis, statuunt, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: How many images do the Jews set up in their cities, let alone their temples, according to Tacitus?
derivation: Jewish aniconism. Anchored to the Jews + Tacitus; single answer 'nulla', supported verbatim by 'nulla simulacra urbibus suis, nedum templis sistunt'. Closed-book ethnographic fact (parallels the Germania 'Nullas ... urbes' structure).

author: Tacitus
source_text: Magna pars Iudaeae vicis dispergitur, habent et oppida; Hierosolyma genti caput. Illic immensae opulentiae templum, et primis munimentis urbs, dein regia, templum intimis clausum.
question: Quae urbs Iudaeae genti caput est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which city is the capital of the Jewish people, according to Tacitus?
derivation: Anchored to the Jewish people + Tacitus; single named city, supported verbatim by 'Hierosolyma genti caput'. Closed-book: Jerusalem as the Jews' chief city and temple-city is universally known.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Romanorum primus Cn. Pompeius Iudaeos domuit templumque iure victoriae ingressus est: inde vulgatum nulla intus deum effigie vacuam sedem et inania arcana.
question: Quis Romanorum primus Iudaeos domuit et templum Hierosolymorum ingressus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Who was the first of the Romans to subdue the Jews and enter the temple of Jerusalem, according to Tacitus?
derivation: Pompey's capture of Jerusalem (63 BC) and entry into the Temple. Anchored to the Jews/Temple + 'Romanorum primus'; single named person, supported verbatim by 'Romanorum primus Cn. Pompeius Iudaeos domuit templumque ... ingressus est'. Closed-book historical fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Qui ubi fato aut taedio occidit, missu Neronis Vespasianus fortuna famaque et egregiis ministris intra duas aestates cuncta camporum omnisque praeter Hierosolyma urbis victore exercitu tenebat.
question: Cuius missu Vespasianus bellum Iudaicum gessit, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: By whose dispatch did Vespasian wage the Jewish war, according to Tacitus?
derivation: Nero appointed Vespasian to the Jewish command. Anchored to Vespasian + the Jewish war; single named person in the genitive ('cuius missu' / 'Neronis'), supported verbatim by 'missu Neronis Vespasianus'. Closed-book: Nero's commissioning of Vespasian against the Jews is a stock fact. (Within two summers he held all but Jerusalem.)

author: Tacitus
source_text: Multitudinem obsessorum omnis aetatis, virile ac muliebre secus, sexcenta milia fuisse accepimus: arma cunctis, qui ferre possent, et plures quam pro numero audebant.
question: Quot milia hominum Hierosolymis obsessa fuisse Tacitus accepit?
question_en: How many thousands of people does Tacitus record were besieged at Jerusalem?
derivation: Number of the besieged at Jerusalem. Anchored to the siege of Jerusalem + Tacitus; single number answer, supported verbatim by 'sexcenta milia fuisse accepimus'. Indirect statement governed by accepit ('accepimus' marks the reported figure). Closed-book number fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Civilis haud porrecto agmine, sed cuneis adstitit: Batavi Cugernique in dextro, laeva ac propiora flumini Transrhenani tenuere.
question: Quis dux barbarorum aciem cuneis instruxit, cuius in dextro cornu Batavi steterunt, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which leader of the barbarians drew up his battle line in wedges, with the Batavi standing on his right wing, according to Tacitus?
derivation: Iulius Civilis, leader of the Batavian revolt against Rome. Anchored to the Batavi (named on his right wing) + Tacitus; single named leader, supported verbatim by 'Civilis ... cuneis adstitit: Batavi Cugernique in dextro'. Closed-book: Civilis is the famous leader of the Batavian revolt (AD 69-70); Book 5 names him simply 'Civilis' (full name Iulius Civilis in the earlier books).

author: Tacitus
source_text: Multa luce revecti hostes captivis navibus, praetoriam triremem flumine Lupia donum Veledae traxere.
question: Cui Germani praetoriam triremem captam, flumine Lupia subvectam, dono dederunt, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: To whom did the Germans give the captured praetorian trireme, brought up the river Lippe, as a gift, according to Tacitus?
derivation: The captured flagship dragged up the Lupia (Lippe) as a gift for the prophetess Veleda. Anchored to the Germans + the trireme; single named person in the dative, supported verbatim by 'praetoriam triremem flumine Lupia donum Veledae traxere'. Closed-book: Veleda, the Bructeran seeress (cf. Germania 8), is a well-known figure.
